Chapter Three: The Disciples At that time, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

"I am stricken with this illness and lie prostrate upon my bed. Does the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, not deign to show me pity, such that he has not sent anyone to inquire after my illness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts and out of compassion for him, addressed Śāriputra:
"You should go to where Vimalakīrti is and inquire after his illness."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not capable of going to him to inquire about his illness.”

Why is this? I recall that once, while I was sitting in meditative seclusion beneath a tree in a great forest, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words: "O Śāriputra!..."
It is not necessarily sitting that constitutes "sitting in repose.
As for sitting in repose: to manifest neither body nor mind within the three realms is sitting in repose;
to manifest all dignified postures without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation is sitting in repose.
To manifest all the phenomena of ordinary beings without abandoning the characteristics of all that has been realized is to sit in meditation;
for the mind to dwell neither within nor proceed without is to sit in meditation;
to abide in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without departing from any of the various views is to sit in meditation.
To not abandon birth and death while remaining free from afflictions, and though realizing nirvana, to have no place of abiding—this is the true practice of sitting in meditation.
If one can sit in meditation in this manner, it is approved by the Buddha.
"At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I remained silent and unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that once, at a certain time, I entered the city of Vaiśālī and was expounding the essentials of the Dharma to various lay devotees at a crossroads.
At that moment, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and said this:
"O Mahāmaudgalyāyana!..."
"When preaching the Dharma to lay devotees, one should not preach as the Venerable has done; rather, one who preaches the Dharma should preach in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, I asked:
"What is meant by preaching in accordance with the Dharma?"
He replied: "The Dharma has no self, for it is free from the defilement of the self;
the Dharma has no sentient beings, for it is free from the dust of emotion."
Dharmas have no life-principle, for they are free from birth and death;
dharmas have no person (pudgala), for their prior and posterior limits are severed;
dharmas are eternally quiescent, for all marks (lakṣaṇa) have been extinguished.
The Dharma is free from attachment, for it has no object of perception;
the Dharma is without letters, for all speech is cut off;
the Dharma is beyond metaphorical explanation, for it is far removed from all surging waves of thought.
The Dharma pervades all things, for it is like space;
the Dharma has no manifestation, being signless and formless, and is far removed from all activities and affairs;
the Dharma is without "mine," for it is free from the notion of possession.
Dharmas have no discernment, for they are apart from mind and consciousness;
dharmas have no comparison, for they are without mutual dependence;
dharmas do not belong to causes, for they do not abide in conditions.
Dharmas are identical to the dharma-realm, because they equally enter the true dharma-realm of all things;
dharmas accord with suchness, because there is nothing to which they accord;
dharmas abide in the limit of reality, because they are ultimately immovable.
Dharmas are without movement, for they do not rely on the six sense objects;
dharmas have no coming or going, for they have no place of abiding;
dharmas accord with emptiness, follow signlessness, and correspond to wishlessness, for they are far removed from all thoughts of increase or decrease.
Dharmas are without acceptance or rejection, for they are free from arising and ceasing;
dharmas are without grasping or storage, for they transcend all paths of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
dharmas are without high or low, for they are eternally abiding and immovable.
The Dharma transcends all that is traversed by conceptual discrimination, for all proliferations (*prapañca*) have been utterly severed.
Indeed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Such is the nature of the Dharma; how could it be expressed in words?
Now, those who preach the Dharma all engage in superimposition and denial;
likewise, those who listen to the Dharma also all engage in superimposition and denial.
Where there is neither increase nor decrease, in that very place there is nothing at all that can be spoken, nothing that can be heard, and nothing that can be cognized.
Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
For example, it is like a conjured being preaching the various dharmas for other conjured beings; one should dwell with such a mind to preach the Dharma.

One should skillfully understand the differences in the faculties and natures of all sentient beings, and with wondrous wisdom, perceive them without obstruction. With great compassion manifesting before them, one should praise and expound the Mahāyāna, mindful of repaying the Buddha’s kindness, with pure intention and skill in dharma and expression, so that the lineage of the Triple Gem may never be severed; only then should one preach the Dharma.
“World-Honored One!
When that great householder preached this Dharma, eight hundred householders within that assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"At that time, World-Honored One, I was silent and unable to respond; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Mahākāśyapa replied,
"World-Honored One!..."
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this?
I recall that once, at a certain time, I entered the city of Vaiśālī and wandered through its poor and humble alleys, going on almsround.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and said:
"O Mahākāśyapa! Although you possess compassion, it is not universal; you abandon the wealthy and noble to beg from the poor."
Venerable Kāśyapa!

One who dwells in the dharma of equanimity should go on almsround in due order; one should go on almsround for the sake of non-eating, one should go on almsround for the sake of destroying attachment to food, and one should go on almsround for the sake of receiving the food offered by others.

One should enter a village with the perception of it as an empty hamlet; one should enter various towns and cities desiring to bring to maturity men and women, both great and small; one should approach the houses of those from whom one begs for alms with the thought of approaching the family of the Buddha, and one should accept that food only for the sake of non-attachment.

Forms seen are like those of the blind; sounds heard are like echoes; odors smelled are like the wind; tastes experienced are not discriminated; tactile sensations received are like the realization of wisdom; and all phenomena are known to be like illusions—devoid of intrinsic nature, devoid of extrinsic nature, without burning, and without extinction.
Venerable Kāśyapa!

If one can enter the eight liberations without abandoning the eight wrong paths, enter right equanimity through the equanimity of the wrong, and offer a single morsel of food to all beings as an offering to the Buddhas and the assembly of noble sages, only then may one eat.

In this way, one may eat only when the eater is neither defiled nor free from defilement, neither entering meditative concentration nor emerging from it, and neither abiding in saṃsāra nor abiding in nirvāṇa. Only then may one eat.

Whatever food is given to the Venerable One bears neither small fruit nor great fruit; it involves neither decrease nor increase, for it leads toward the path of the Buddha and does not lead toward the path of the Śrāvakas.
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
If one can eat food in such a manner, one does not eat the food given by others in vain.
"At that time, World-Honored One!"
Hearing these words, he attained what he had never experienced before and immediately conceived a profound sense of reverence for all the bodhisattvas.
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!

That a householder such as this possesses such eloquence and wisdom is truly marvelous. What person of intelligence, upon hearing such a teaching, would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"

Since that time, I have not encouraged sentient beings to seek the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; I have taught them only to resolve their minds toward and seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Subhūti:
"You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Then, the Great Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that once, at one time, I entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for alms and subsequently entered her house.
At that time, Vimalā paid homage to me, took my bowl, filled it with excellent food, and said to me:
"Venerable Subhūti!..."

If one can enter into the equality of all phenomena through the equality of food, and through the equality of all phenomena enter into the equality of all Buddhas—only one who can do so may take the food.

"Venerable Subhūti! If you can neither sever nor be accompanied by greed, hatred, and delusion; if you can enter the path of the single destination without destroying the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); if you can give rise to wisdom and liberation without extinguishing ignorance and craving for existence; if you can enter the state of equality of liberation through the uninterrupted nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—which is neither liberated nor bound; if you do not perceive the Four Truths, yet are not one who does not perceive the Truths or attain the fruit; if you are neither an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) nor separated from the dharmas of an ordinary being, neither a noble (*ārya*) nor not a noble—if, while accomplishing all dharmas, you remain free from the conceptualization of dharmas, then you may accept this food."
"Venerable Subhūti, if you do not see the Buddha,

do not hear the Dharma, and do not serve the Saṃgha— and if those six teachers of the non-Buddhists— Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra— were your teachers under whom you went forth as a renunciant, and if those six teachers have fallen, you too have fallen— only then may you accept this food."

Venerable Subhūti, if one falls into various views and reaches neither the middle nor the extremes; if one enters the eight unfavorable conditions and fails to obtain the favorable; if one shares in all defilements and remains apart from purity;
and if one attains the state of non-contention that all sentient beings have attained—then, Venerable One, you too would not be called a pure field of merit.
Those who offer food to the Venerable One fall into the evil realms; for by doing so, they join hands with the various Māras and take the afflictions as their companions.

"The very nature of all afflictions is the very nature of the Venerable One—conceiving thoughts of enmity and harm toward all sentient beings, slandering all Buddhas, disparaging all dharmas, not being included within the ranks of the Saṃgha, and never having the time for final parinirvāṇa—if you are thus, then you may take this food."

"At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I was as if shrouded in dense darkness and lost my sense of direction; I did not know what those words meant, nor did I know how to answer. I then set aside my bowl and wished to leave his house."
Then Vimalakīrti said to me:
"Venerable Subhūti!
Take the bowl; do not be afraid."
"What do you think?
If it were an emanation created by the Tathāgatas, would there be any fear if one were to interrogate it with such matters? I replied:
"No," Vimalakīrti replied.

"The nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; the nature and characteristics of all sentient beings and all verbal expressions are likewise so. Therefore, those who possess wisdom should not cling to words nor should they harbor fear toward them."
Why is this so? Because all verbal expressions are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics.
For what reason?
"The nature and characteristics of all words and letters are also transcended; they are not words at all, and this is liberation.
The characteristic of liberation is precisely all dharmas.
"World-Honored One!"
When that great householder taught this Dharma, twenty thousand devaputras became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
five hundred devaputras attained the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti).
At that time, I remained silent, suddenly losing my eloquence and being unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“You should go to Vimalakīrti’s dwelling to inquire after his illness.”
Then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that once, while I was in a great forest preaching the Dharma to a group of newly ordained bhikṣus,
Vimalakīrti came to that place, prostrated at my feet, and spoke as follows:
"O Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
You should first enter meditative concentration and observe the minds of these bhikṣus, and only then should you preach the Dharma for them.
Do not place foul food into a precious vessel; you should first understand what the inclinations of these bhikṣus are."
Do not treat priceless *vaiḍūrya* gems as if they were common, fragile, and base crystal beads. Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Do not fail to examine the differences in the faculties of sentient beings before bestowing upon them a teaching suited only for those of inferior faculties; do not wound those who are already free of sores. Those who wish to travel the Great Road should not be shown a narrow path. Do not equate the light of the sun with that of a firefly; do not attempt to contain the great ocean within the footprint of an ox; do not place Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, inside a mustard seed; and do not equate the roar of a great lion with the cry of a jackal.
Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

These bhikṣus all set out upon the Mahāyāna in the past and directed their minds toward awakening, yet they have forgotten this intention in the interim; how can you show them the vehicle of the śrāvakas?

I observe that the wisdom of the śrāvakas is so feeble and shallow as to surpass even one born blind; they lack the sublime wisdom of the Mahāyāna that contemplates the faculties of sentient beings, and are thus unable to distinguish whether the faculties of all sentient beings are sharp or dull.

Then, by means of such a sublime samādhi, Vimalakīrti caused the bhikṣus to recollect their various past lives in detail—how they had planted roots of goodness in the presence of five hundred Buddhas in the past, accumulated immeasurable and supreme merits, and dedicated them toward the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Once they had recollected these matters of their past lives, the aspiration for enlightenment reappeared before them, and they immediately prostrated at the feet of that Mahāsattva.
Then Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for him, causing him to become non-retrogressive from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"At that time, World-Honored One,
I had this thought:"

"Those who are śrāvakas do not know the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings; they must not, without having informed the Tathāgata, suddenly preach the Dharma to others on their own initiative. Why is this so?"

The various śrāvakas do not know the superior or inferior faculties of sentient beings, nor are they constantly in meditative concentration like the Buddha, the World-Honored One; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākātyāyana:
"You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Kātyāyana replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that once, after the Buddha had briefly taught the Dharma to the bhikṣus and entered into meditative seclusion, I subsequently analyzed and determined the meaning of the sūtra passages—namely, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words:
"O Great Honored One Kātyāyana!
Do not use a mind of conceptual activity characterized by arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark."

Why is this so? That all phenomena are ultimately neither already arisen, nor currently arising, nor yet to arise; neither already ceased, nor currently ceasing, nor yet to cease—this is the meaning of impermanence.
To thoroughly penetrate that the five aggregates are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature and have no basis from which they arise—this is the meaning of suffering.
That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness;
that knowing the self and the absence of self are non-dual is the meaning of selflessness;

that there is neither intrinsic nature nor extrinsic nature, that there was originally no blazing and now no extinguishing, and that there is no tranquility yet ultimate and final tranquility—this is the meaning of cessation.
When this Dharma was spoken, the outflows of those bhikṣus were forever exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
"At that time, World-Honored One, I remained silent and lacked the ability to respond; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahā-Ānanda:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Then Mahā-Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this? Because:”

I recall that once, while I was walking back and forth in a certain place within a great forest, there appeared a Brahmā king named Śuddhāvāsa, accompanied by ten thousand Brahmās. Emitting a great radiance, he approached me, prostrated himself in salutation, and asked me:
"Venerable Aniruddha!..."
"To what extent can the divine eye one has attained see?
At that time, I replied:
"Great Seer, you should know:"
"I am able to see this trichiliocosm, the buddha-field of Śākyamuni, as clearly as if I were looking at an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of my hand.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and said:
"Venerable Aniruddha!..."
Is the divine eye thus attained characterized by mental activity (*sanimitta*) or is it without mental activity (*animitta*)? If it were characterized by mental activity,
it would be equal to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"If that which lacks the characteristic of activity is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it should not possess vision.
How then, World-Honored One, could the divine eye attained by the Venerable One possess the capacity for seeing?
At that time, World-Honored One!
He remained silent and was unable to respond;
however, when those Brahmās heard what he had said, they experienced something unprecedented, immediately prostrated before him, and asked:
"In this world, who has attained the true divine eye?"
Vimalakīrti said:

"There are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who have attained the true divine eye; they behold all Buddha-lands without abandoning meditative concentration, perceiving them neither as dualistic nor as manifold."

At that time, the Brahma King and his five hundred retinues all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they paid homage to Vimalakīrti and suddenly vanished from sight. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Then Upāli said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that once, in the past, there were two bhikṣus who had violated the precepts they had received; deeply ashamed and not daring to approach the Buddha, they came to me, prostrated at my feet, and said to me:
"Venerable Upāli!..."
"Now we two have transgressed the rules of conduct and truly feel ashamed; we do not dare approach the Buddha, but wish to resolve our grief and regret so as to be exempt from this fault.

I then provided them with a Dharma explanation according to the law, causing them to eliminate their grief and regret and purify their transgression, instructing, exhorting, encouraging, and comforting them.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Upāli! Do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus; you should simply eliminate their remorse for what they have committed and do not disturb their minds."
Why is this? That nature of sin does not abide within, nor does it emerge from without, nor does it exist between the two.
As the Buddha has said:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled;
because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified.
Thus, the mind does not abide within, nor does it go without, nor does it exist in between the two.
As is the nature of the mind, so too is the nature of defilements;
as is the nature of defilements, so too is the nature of all phenomena, for they do not transcend suchness. Indeed, Upāli!
"Is this originally pure mind of yours ever defiled at the time you attain liberation? I replied, "No."
Vimalakīrti said:
"The nature of the minds of all sentient beings is fundamentally pure and has never been defiled;
it is just like this. Indeed, Upāli!"
If there is conceptualization and diverse conceptualization, there is affliction; if there is no conceptualization and no diverse conceptualization, that is intrinsic purity.
If there is inversion, there is affliction; if there is no inversion, that is intrinsic purity.
If there is grasping at a self, defilement arises; if there is no grasping at a self, that is intrinsic purity.
"Indeed, Upāli!
The nature of all dharmas arises and ceases without abiding; they are like illusions, like transformations, like lightning, and like clouds.
The nature of all dharmas does not depend upon one another; they do not abide for even a single thought-moment."
The nature of all phenomena is a false perception, like a dream, a mirage, or a city of the gandharvas;
the nature of all phenomena is a reflection produced by the discriminating mind, like the moon in water or an image in a mirror.
"One who knows thus is called one who well upholds the Vinaya; one who knows thus is called one who is well-disciplined.
When the two bhikṣus heard this teaching, they attained what they had never experienced before and both said:
"How marvelous, householder!"

He possesses such supreme wisdom and eloquence that even Upāli cannot equal him; though the Buddha declared Upāli to be the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, he was unable to explain it as this one does.
I then said to him:
"Do not conceive the notion that he is a householder. Why is this so?"
Except for the Tathāgata, no śrāvaka or other bodhisattva has ever been able to restrain the wisdom and eloquence of this Great Being; such is the clarity and excellence of his wisdom and eloquence.
At that time, the two bhikṣus’ remorse was immediately dispelled, and they both gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. They then paid homage and made this aspiration:
"May all sentient beings attain such sublime wisdom and eloquence."
"At that time, I remained silent and was unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula:
"You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
Then Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that once, in the past, there were some young boys of the Licchavi clan who came to where I was, prostrated themselves in greeting, and asked me:
"Venerable Rāhula!..."
"You are the son of a Buddha; you have renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and pursue the path.
What are the merits and benefits of such renunciation?
I then explained to him, in accordance with the Dharma, the merits and benefits of leaving the household life.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words:
"O Rāhula! You should not proclaim the merits and benefits of renunciation in such a manner."
Why is this? Because there is no merit and no benefit—this is what constitutes going forth. Indeed, Rāhula!
Within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one may speak of virtues and benefits;
however, for one who has gone forth, there is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and within the unconditioned, it is impossible to speak of virtues or benefits.
"O Rāhula! For one who has gone forth, there is neither 'that' nor 'this,' nor anything in between.
To be far removed from all views, being neither form nor non-form—this is the path to Nirvāṇa."
Praised by the wise and embraced by the noble ones, they subdue all Māras, transcend the five destinies, purify and cultivate the five eyes, establish the five faculties, and realize the five powers.
He does not afflict others, remains free from all unwholesome dharmas, subdues all non-Buddhists, and transcends provisional designations.

Having emerged from the mire of desire, he is without attachment or grasping; he is free from "I" and "mine," devoid of all forms of clinging, and has already severed all clinging. He is without agitation, having already severed agitation; he skillfully disciplines his own mind and skillfully protects the minds of others. He accords with tranquility (*śamatha*) and diligently cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*); he abandons all evil and cultivates all that is wholesome.
"If one can act in this way, it is called true renunciation.
Then Vimalakīrti said to the youths:
"You should now all go forth together within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya."

"Why is this? It is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; it is difficult to be free from the states of non-leisure; and it is difficult to obtain a human body. To be fully endowed with leisure is the foremost and most difficult of all.
The youths said:
"O Great Householder!
I have heard the Buddha say that one may not leave the household life without the permission of one's parents.
Vimalakīrti replied:

"You youths, simply give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and diligently cultivate right practice; this itself is renunciation, and this itself is the reception of full ordination that constitutes the nature of a bhikṣu."
At that time, the thirty-two Licchavi youths all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and vowed to practice the correct path.
I remained silent and was unable to offer further eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Then Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this? Because—”
I recall that once, at one time, the World-Honored One’s body manifested a slight ailment for which he required cow’s milk.
In the early morning, having adjusted my usual robes and taking up my bowl and outer garment, I went to the house of a brahmin in Vaiśālī and stood at the gate to beg for cow’s milk.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and said: "Venerable Ānanda,
why are you here at dawn holding your alms bowl?"
I said: "Householder!
The World-Honored One has a slight ailment in his body; it is for the purpose of using cow's milk that I have come here."
Then Vimalakīrti said to me:
"Stop, stop, Venerable One!
Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. Do not defame the Tathāgata with false matters."

Why is this so? Because the body of the Tathāgata is composed of adamant; all unwholesome dharmas, along with their habitual tendencies, have been forever severed, and all wholesome dharmas have been fully perfected and accomplished.
What illness could there be?
What affliction could there be? Indeed, Ānanda!

He returned silently to his dwelling, lest any other person hear these coarse words, and so that the gods of great majesty and virtue, as well as the bodhisattvas who have come from other buddha-fields, might not hear such speech.
"Indeed, Ānanda!

If even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, who has accomplished only a small portion of accumulated roots of goodness, attains freedom from illness, how much more so the Tathāgata, whose immeasurable roots of goodness and merit-wisdom are perfectly fulfilled—could he possibly have any ailment?"
"It is absolutely impossible. Venerable Ānanda!
You must go quickly in silence; do not cause us to suffer such ignominy."
If the non-Buddhist Brahmins and others were to hear these harsh words, they would think:
"What kind of teacher is this?
He cannot even cure his own illness; how then could he cure the illnesses of others?"
"You must depart secretly and swiftly so that no one hears of it. Furthermore, Ānanda!

The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, not a body of impurity; it is a supramundane body, unsullied by worldly dharmas; it is an outflow-free body, free from all outflows; it is an unconditioned body, free from all conditioned things; it transcends all numerical categories, for all numbers are eternally stilled."
"How could such a Buddha-body have any illness?
"At that time, World-Honored One,
having heard these words, I was truly filled with shame and remorse."
"Could it be that I have heard erroneously because I am too close to the Buddha?
Immediately, a voice was heard from the air, saying: "You, Ānanda!"

As the householder has said, the true body of the World-Honored One is indeed free from illness; it is only because the Tathāgata has appeared in this world of five turbidities that he manifests such a thing in order to transform and guide sentient beings who are impoverished, afflicted by suffering, and of evil conduct.
"Go, Ānanda! Take the milk; do not be ashamed.
"At that time, World-Honored One!"

Having heard that Great Being’s exposition of such eloquence, I did not know what he was saying and remained silent, unable to offer a reply; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.
In this manner, the World-Honored One addressed each of the five hundred great disciples among the śrāvakas individually, saying:
“You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.”
Each of these śrāvakas recounted their own past causes and conditions to the Buddha, praising the words of the Great Being Vimalakīrti, and all said:
"We are not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."
Chapter 4: The Bodhisattvas. From the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Four, "The Bodhisattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness."

Why is this? I recall that at one time, for the sake of the King of Tuṣita Heaven and his retinue, I expounded the essential teachings regarding all the stages of non-retrogression belonging to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Maitreya!
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed upon you the prediction that, being bound by only one more birth, you shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
By means of which birth does one receive the prediction?
Is it in the past,
or is it in the future?
Is it present?
If it were a past birth, that past birth has already ceased;
if it were a future birth, that future birth has not yet arrived.
If there is arising in the present, that arising in the present has no duration.
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, moment by moment you are endowed with birth, old age, and death; you perish and are born again."

If one receives the prediction of enlightenment by means of non-arising, then non-arising itself is the very state of rightness into which one enters; within this state of rightness that is entered—non-arising—there is no prediction, nor is there any realization of perfect, complete enlightenment.
How is it, Maitreya! Is one granted the prediction [of enlightenment] by means of attaining it?
Or is one granted the prediction by relying on the way things arise?
Is it by depending on the extinction of suchness that one receives the prediction?
If one were to receive the prediction by depending on the arising of suchness, suchness has no arising;
if one were to receive the prediction by depending on the extinction of suchness, suchness has no extinction.
Within the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), which is without arising and without cessation, there is no bestowing of prophecy.
All sentient beings are suchness; all phenomena are suchness; all noble ones and sages are suchness; and even Maitreya is suchness.
If the Venerable Maitreya were to receive a prophecy of enlightenment, then all sentient beings should likewise receive such a prophecy.
Why is this? For True Suchness (tathatā) is not manifested as dual, nor is it manifested through various distinct natures.
If the Venerable Maitreya shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then all sentient beings should likewise realize it. Why is this?
Now, as for bodhi, it is that which all sentient beings equally awaken to.
If the Venerable Maitreya were to enter parinirvāṇa, then all sentient beings would likewise have to enter nirvāṇa.
Why is this? It is not that all sentient beings do not attain parinirvāṇa.

The Buddha taught that True Suchness (tathatā) is parinirvāṇa; because the Buddha perceives that the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is quiescent, which is the very characteristic of nirvāṇa, he therefore teaches that True Suchness is parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, Maitreya!
Do not entice the sons of the gods with this Dharma; do not cause the sons of the gods to be hindered by this Dharma.
For as for Bodhi, there is no seeking after it, nor is there any retrogression from it.
“Venerable Maitreya!
You should cause these sons of the gods to relinquish their conceptual views regarding bodhi. Why is this so?
Now, as for bodhi, it cannot be realized by the body, nor can it be realized by the mind.
Quiescence is bodhi, because all sentient beings and all dharmic characteristics are quiescent;
non-increase is bodhi, because no objects of perception are augmented.
Non-engagement is enlightenment, because all conceptual proliferation and all mental engagements are not engaged;
perpetual severance is enlightenment, because all dogmatic views are perpetually severed;
relinquishment is enlightenment, because all grasping and attachment are relinquished.
Enlightenment is freedom from fetters, for it is forever free from all agitated phenomena;
enlightenment is tranquility, for all conceptual discrimination is forever stilled;
enlightenment is vastness, for its great vows are immeasurable.
Non-contention is enlightenment, for it is free from all attachments and all disputes;
abiding is enlightenment, for it dwells within the dharma-realm;
following along is enlightenment, for it accords with suchness.
Non-duality is bodhi, because it is utterly free from all differentiated dharmas;
establishment is bodhi, because it is established upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
equality is bodhi, because everything from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental objects is entirely equal, like space.
Unconditioned is bodhi, because it is ultimately free from arising, abiding, change, and cessation;
all-knowing is bodhi, because one thoroughly knows all the mental activities of all sentient beings;
uninterrupted is bodhi, because it is not intermingled with the six internal sense bases and so forth.
Enlightenment is without admixture, because it is forever free from the continuity of all afflictions and their habitual tendencies;
enlightenment is without location, because within suchness it is removed from all spatial dimensions;
enlightenment is without abiding, because it cannot be perceived in any place whatsoever.
Enlightenment is merely a name, for this enlightenment is devoid of functional activity;
enlightenment is waveless, for it is forever free from all grasping and rejecting;
enlightenment is undisturbed, for it is eternally quiescent.
Excellent tranquility is bodhi, because its fundamental nature is pure;
clarity is bodhi, because its self-nature is without admixture;
non-appropriation is bodhi, because it is free from objective reference.
Bodhi is without distinction, because it awakens to the equality of all phenomena;
Bodhi is beyond metaphor, because it is forever free from all analogies;
Bodhi is subtle and wondrous, because it is extremely difficult to awaken to.
All-pervasive is bodhi, for its intrinsic nature is all-encompassing like space;
reaching the summit is bodhi, for it reaches the highest pinnacle among all phenomena;
unstained is bodhi, for no worldly phenomena can defile it.
"In this way, bodhi cannot be realized by the body, nor can it be realized by the mind.
"World-Honored One!
When that great householder preached this Dharma, two hundred devaputras among the assembly of gods attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
"At that time, I remained silent and was unable to offer further argument; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Prabhāvyūha:
"You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his health."
The youth Prabhāvyūha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
Why is this? I recall that once, at a certain time, I was departing from the city of Vaiśālī when Vimalakīrti was entering that very city. I paid him homage and asked:
"Householder, from where have you come?"
He replied to me, saying:
"From the wondrous Bodhi. I asked:
"Householder!
What is this so-called 'sublime enlightenment'?
He then replied to me, saying:
"Sincere intention is the sublime bodhi, because this intention is not artificial;
the initiation of application is the sublime bodhi, because all that is undertaken can be accomplished;
the superior intention is the sublime bodhi, because it ultimately realizes the supreme Dharma."
The great bodhicitta is the sublime bodhi, for it never forgets any dharma;
pure generosity is the sublime bodhi, for it does not hope for worldly karmic results;
steadfastly maintaining pure ethical discipline is the sublime bodhi, for all aspirations and requests are thereby fulfilled.
Patience and gentleness are the sublime awakening, for the mind harbors no malice toward sentient beings;
courageous diligence is the sublime awakening, for one practices with fervent application without slackening or retreat;
tranquility and meditative concentration are the sublime awakening, for the mind is disciplined, compliant, and capable.
Exalted Prajñā is the sublime bodhi, because it directly perceives the nature and characteristics of all phenomena;
loving-kindness is the sublime bodhi, because the mind is impartial toward all sentient beings;
compassion is the sublime bodhi, because it is able to endure all weariness and suffering.
Joy is the sublime bodhi, for it constantly experiences the bliss of the Dharma garden;
equanimity is the sublime bodhi, for it forever severs all attachment, aversion, and the like;
the supernormal powers are the sublime bodhi, for they possess the six supernormal powers.
Liberation is sublime bodhi, for it is free from the movement of conceptual discrimination;
skillful means are sublime bodhi, for they bring sentient beings to maturity;
the articles of attraction are sublime bodhi, for they gather in all sentient beings.
Extensive learning is the sublime bodhi, because it gives rise to practice based on reality;
self-discipline is the sublime bodhi, because it involves observation according to principle;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the sublime bodhi, because they involve relinquishing all conditioned phenomena.
All truths are the sublime bodhi, for they are not deceptive toward sentient beings;
the twelve links of dependent origination are the sublime bodhi, for ignorance is not exhausted, nor are aging, death, sorrow, suffering, and affliction exhausted;
the cessation of all afflictions is the sublime bodhi, for one realizes the true nature of phenomena as it is.
All sentient beings are the sublime bodhi, for they all take non-self as their intrinsic nature;
all dharmas are the sublime bodhi, for one awakens to them all as being empty of self-nature;
subduing the demonic adversaries is the sublime bodhi, for all demonic adversaries cannot cause it to waver.
Not departing from the three realms is the sublime bodhi, because it is far removed from all undertakings;
the great lion’s roar is the sublime bodhi, because it is able to skillfully discern with fearlessness;
the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-dharmas are the sublime bodhi, because they are universally free from reproach or aversion toward anything.
The three types of higher knowledge (vidyā) illuminate this wondrous bodhi; by being free from all afflictions, one attains ultimate, exhaustive wisdom.

Therefore, the awakening to all phenomena in a single moment of mind as being ultimately and exhaustively so is wondrous bodhi, because it is the perfect realization of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
In this way, noble son!

If bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the genuine aspiration for enlightenment, fully endowed with the perfections (*pāramitā*), fully endowed with the maturation of sentient beings, fully endowed with all roots of goodness, fully endowed with the upholding of the true Dharma, and fully endowed with the making of offerings to the Tathāgatas—then whatever they do, whether coming or going, advancing or stopping, lifting or setting down their feet—all proceeds from the sublime Bodhi and all proceeds from the teachings of all Buddhas, as they abide securely in the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
When that great householder preached this Dharma, five hundred devaputras all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
At that time, I remained silent and was unable to offer further eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Lokadhara:
"You should go to the dwelling of Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
The Bodhisattva Lokadhara replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that once, while I was dwelling in my own abode, the evil Māra, the adversary, accompanied by twelve thousand celestial maidens who appeared like Śakra, arrived at my place with music, stringed instruments, and song. Together with his retinue, he prostrated at my feet, performed various celestial musical offerings for me, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
At that time, I thought he was truly Śakra and said to him: "Welcome, Kauśika!

Although you possess merit, you ought not to be self-indulgent; you should diligently observe that all the pleasures of desire are impermanent, and you should earnestly cultivate yourself in body, life, and wealth to realize the firm and substantial Dharma."
He then said to me:
"O Great Noble Being!
You may accept this woman to serve you."
I immediately replied: "Stop, Kauśika!
Do not offer such unrighteous things to me, a śramaṇa disciple of the Śākya; this is not appropriate for me."
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti arrived at that place, prostrated at my feet, and said to me:
"This is not Śakra; it is the Evil Māra, who has come merely to trouble you."
Then Vimalakīrti said to Māra, "You should now offer these goddesses to me;
they are appropriate for me as a layman in white robes, but they are not for śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, to accept."
At that moment, the evil Māra was struck with terror and thought,
"Vimalakīrti will surely trouble me.
He wished to vanish and depart.
Sustained by the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti, they could not remain hidden; even though they exhausted all their powers and employed various skillful means, they were unable to depart.
Then, a voice was heard from the sky, saying:
"You, Evil Māra, enemy of the world, must give these celestial maidens to this layman before you may return to your own heavenly palace."
"Out of fear, this evil Māra, the enemy, reluctantly gave them to me. Then Vimalakīrti said to the women,
"Since this evil Māra, the enemy, has given you to me as alms, sisters, you should now resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
He then taught them various methods for maturing toward sublime enlightenment as was appropriate for each, leading them toward perfect, equal enlightenment.
He further said:

"Sisters, you have already resolved upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; you possess the great pleasure of the garden of Dharma with which you may delight yourselves, and you should no longer take pleasure in the pleasures of the five desires."
The celestial maidens said:
"O Great Householder!
What is meant by 'the joy of the great garden of Dharma'?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"The joy of the Dharma garden consists of the joy of unshakable pure faith in all Buddhas, the joy of constantly hearing the true Dharma,
the joy of diligently and respectfully serving the harmonious Saṃgha, and the joy of eternal transcendence from the three realms."
the joy of being without dependence or dwelling upon any objects of perception; the joy of contemplating the aggregates as impermanent and like harmful enemies;
the joy of correctly observing the elements as being like venomous snakes;
the joy of correctly observing the sense bases as being like an empty village; the joy of firmly guarding the bodhicitta; and at...
The joy of benefiting all sentient beings; the joy of diligently serving and attending upon teachers and elders;

the joy of being free from stinginess and greed regarding generosity; the joy of being without laxity or negligence regarding pure ethical discipline; the joy of being capable and compliant regarding patience;
the joy of cultivating roots of virtue regarding diligence; and the knowledge of non-distraction regarding meditative concentration.
The joy of being free from delusion within *prajñā*; the joy of vast and sublime bliss within *bodhi*;
the joy of being able to subjugate all demonic adversaries; the joy of thoroughly knowing all afflictions (*kleśa*);
the joy of universally cultivating and purifying all Buddha-fields; and the joy of perfect fulfillment within the body adorned with the primary marks and secondary signs.
The joy of correctly cultivating the two provisions of merit and wisdom; the joy of being adorned with sublime enlightenment;
the joy of having no fear or alarm regarding the profound Dharma; the joy of correctly contemplating the three gates of liberation;
the joy of correctly taking *parinirvāṇa* as one's object of focus; the joy of not contemplating at an improper time; and [the joy] regarding those who are equal...

They find joy in constantly associating with those of similar birth who perceive their virtues; they find joy in being free from malice toward those of different birth whom they do not perceive as having faults;
they find joy in associating with all virtuous friends; they find joy in protecting all evil associates;
they find joy in skillfully gathering others through expedient means; and they find joy in faith and delight within all dharmas.
In heedfulness, one cultivates all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*),
which is the most supreme and sublime bliss. Thus, sisters,
this is the great pleasure of the Dharma-garden for a bodhisattva.
"This is the joy of the Dharma-grove, wherein all great bodhisattvas constantly dwell; you should take delight in this, and not in the pleasures of desire.
Then the evil Māra, the adversary, said to the goddesses:
"Come here! I now wish to return with you all to the celestial palace."
The women replied:
"Evil Māra, depart! We shall no longer return with you. Why is this? Because—"
"Since you have given us to this householder, how can we possibly return to you?
We now delight in the joy of the Dharma-grove and no longer delight in the pleasures of desire; you may return alone."
Then the evil Māra, the adversary, said to Vimalakīrti:
"O Great Householder!
You should relinquish these women; for one who bestows all that they possess without the mind being attached to them is a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Vimalakīrti said, "I have already relinquished them;
you may take them away, and I shall cause all sentient beings such as yourselves to have their aspirations for the Dharma fulfilled."
Then the celestial maidens prostrated before Vimalakīrti and asked him, saying:
"O Great Householder!
Once we have returned to the palace of Māra, how should we practice?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"Sisters, you should know that there is a sublime Dharma-gate called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp'; you should all study it."
The goddess asked again:
"What is meant by the 'inexhaustible lamp'?
He replied:
"Sisters! It is like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps; all that was dark becomes bright, yet the light is never exhausted, nor does it diminish.
In this same way, sisters!"

If a single bodhisattva encourages and establishes hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings so that they seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, the bodhicitta of that bodhisattva will never be exhausted, nor will it diminish; rather, it will increase even further.
In this way, by skillfully expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of others, one's own wholesome qualities increase further and further, never coming to an end and never declining.
Sisters, you should know:
this sublime Dharma gate is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp," and you should study it.

Even while dwelling in the palace of Māra, you should exhort immeasurable sons and daughters of the gods to resolve upon Bodhicitta; thus, you will be said to truly repay the kindness of the Tathāgata, and you will also bring benefit to all sentient beings.
These celestial maidens paid their respects and prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti.

At that moment, Vimalakīrti relinquished the supernatural power he had previously employed to subdue the Māra king; consequently, the Māra, along with his retinue, suddenly vanished and returned to his own palace.
“World-Honored One!

Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign spiritual powers, wisdom, and eloquence, and manifests such transformations while preaching the Dharma; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder’s son Sudatta, saying:
“You should go to the place of Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.
Then Sudatta replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness. Why is this? Because—”

I recall that in the past, within my own father’s house, for seven days and seven nights, I held a great sacrificial assembly, making offerings to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and various non-Buddhists, as well as to the poor, the lowly, the solitary, and beggars.
When this great sacrifice had reached its seventh day, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me:
"O son of a householder!
A sacrificial assembly should not be conducted by you as it is currently being arranged here."
"You should now arrange a sacrificial assembly of the Dharma; what use is such a sacrificial assembly of material wealth?
I said, "Householder!"
"What is called the sacrificial assembly of the gift of Dharma?
He replied to me:

"The sacrificial assembly of the gift of Dharma is that which, without before or after, simultaneously makes offerings to all sentient beings; this is called the perfect sacrificial assembly of the gift of Dharma."
What is that matter? It means:

inducing great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) through the aspect of practicing for unsurpassed enlightenment; inducing great compassion (*karuṇā*) through the aspect of the liberation of all sentient beings;
and inducing great sympathetic joy (*muditā*) through the aspect of rejoicing in all sentient beings.

The aspect of gathering the true Dharma and gathering wisdom gives rise to great equanimity; the aspect of sublime tranquility and subduing gives rise to the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*);
the aspect of transforming sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts gives rise to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
and the aspect of the selflessness of all phenomena gives rise to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
By means of the aspect of skillfully distancing oneself from the activities of body and mind, one brings forth the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
by means of the aspect of supreme factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), one brings forth the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*);
by means of the aspect of hearing all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), one brings forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); and by means of transforming all sentient beings...

One brings forth the cultivation of emptiness by means of the aspect of practice; one brings forth the cultivation of signlessness by means of the aspect of practice that remedies all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*);
one brings forth the cultivation of wishlessness by means of the aspect of intentional rebirth; one brings forth great power by means of the aspect of skillfully upholding the True Dharma;
and one brings forth the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) by means of the aspect of skillfully cultivating the bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*). By means of...
One should cultivate the state of being free from pride by adopting the manner of serving all sentient beings as one's own servants;
one should cultivate the attainment of a firm body, life, and wealth by trading that which is insubstantial for that which is substantial;
one should cultivate right mindfulness by means of the six modes of recollection; and one should cultivate [the path] by means of practicing the pure and sublime dharmas.
One should inspire pure livelihood through the aspect of practicing right conduct with diligence;

inspire the service and attendance of noble beings through the aspect of approaching them with pure joy; inspire the taming of the mind through the aspect of not harboring malice toward those who are not noble;
and inspire superior purification through the aspect of the perfectly pure life of renunciation.
Through the mental disposition of constantly cultivating the mode of practice of the Middle Way, one elicits skill in means and extensive learning;
through the mode of practice of penetrating the Dharma free from contention, one elicits constant dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*);

through the mode of practice of correctly seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, one elicits meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*); and through the correct pacification of the afflictions of all sentient beings.
He brings forth the mode of practice that thoroughly cultivates the stages of yoga;
he brings forth the mode of practice that matures sentient beings and adorns pure buddha-fields through the possession of the marks and signs;

and he brings forth the mode of practice that knows the mental activities of all sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to their needs, thereby bringing forth the vast and sublime accumulation of wisdom.
By means of the gateway of the single principle of neither grasping nor rejecting any phenomena, one awakens to the mode of practice that engenders the vast accumulation of sublime wisdom;

by means of the mode of practice that severs all obstacles consisting of the latencies of afflictions and all unwholesome dharmas, one engenders the realization and attainment of all wholesome dharmas;
and by means of the awakening to the single [nature] of the knowledge of all-knowledge...
It is the manifestation and realization of all aspects of the provisions for wholesome dharmas and all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) that are cultivated.
O son of good family!
This is what is called the sacrificial assembly of the gift of Dharma.
"If bodhisattvas abide in such a sacrificial assembly of the gift of Dharma, they are called great donors, universally honored by the world of devas and humans.
"World-Honored One! [he continued.]
When that great householder preached this Dharma, two hundred brahmins among the assembly of brahmins all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, I marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and attained pure joy; I paid homage by bowing my head at the feet of that Great Being and respectfully offered him a precious necklace worth hundreds of thousands.
He was unwilling to accept it, so I said:
"O Great Being!
Out of compassion for me, I pray that you will certainly accept it."
"If you do not require it yourself, give it as you please to those whom your heart trusts.

Then Vimalakīrti accepted the necklace, divided it into two portions, gave one portion to the most loathsome, wretched, and lowly beggar in this great sacrificial assembly, and offered the other portion to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.

By means of his supernormal powers, he caused the great assembly to see the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa in the world-system Marīci in another direction; they also saw that one portion of the pearl necklace offered as a gift had become a wondrous jeweled pavilion above that Buddha, with four pavilions on its four sides, symmetrically arranged and adorned with various ornaments, most delightful to behold.
Having manifested such miraculous transformations as these, he further spoke these words:

"If there is a donor who, with a mind of equanimity, gives to the lowliest beggar in this assembly—regarding them with the same thought as one has for the Tathāgata’s field of merit, without discrimination, with an impartial mind, and with great kindness and great compassion—bestowing universally upon all without seeking any karmic reward, this is called the perfect sacrifice of the gift of Dharma."

At that time, this beggar, having witnessed those miraculous transformations and heard what was said, attained the superior intention of non-retrogression and immediately resolved his mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!
That great householder possesses such sovereign supernormal transformations and unimpeded eloquence; therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
In this manner, the World-Honored One addressed each of the great bodhisattvas individually, saying:
"Go to the householder Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Each of these bodhisattvas then related to the Buddha their own past connections with him, praising the words of the mahāsattva Vimalakīrti, and all said:
"I am unable to go to him to inquire after his illness.

Chapter Five: Inquiring after Illness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“You should now go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
That Great Being is difficult to engage in debate; he has entered deeply into the Dharma-gates and is skilled in eloquent exposition. Abiding in wondrous eloquence, his awakened wisdom is unimpeded.

He has already accomplished all the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas. He is able to enter into all the secret realms of the great Bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas. He skillfully subdues all Māras and possesses unhindered, expedient means.

Having already reached the most supreme, non-dual, and unmixed realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and having attained the ultimate further shore of all practice, they are able to expound the Dharma-gate of infinite manifestations within the realm of phenomena adorned with a single characteristic.
He thoroughly understands the faculties and conduct of all sentient beings, skillfully sports with the most supreme supernormal powers, and has reached the stage of great wisdom and skillful means.
Having attained fearlessness and mastery in resolving all questions and answers, he cannot be opposed by the verbal dexterity or sharp rhetoric of any inferior beings.

"Nevertheless, I shall go to him to inquire after his illness by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; once I have arrived there, I shall engage in discourse with him according to my own capacity.
Thereupon, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, and the sons of gods in the assembly all thought to themselves:
"Now these two bodhisattvas both possess profound and vast superior resolve; if they debate with one another, they will certainly proclaim the subtle and wondrous teachings of the Dharma."
"We should now also join together and follow him to that place for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, World-Protectors, and sons of gods within the assembly all requested to go along for the sake of hearing the Dharma.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and the sons of gods, all rose with reverence and prostrated to the World-Honored One. Surrounded by them in front and behind, he departed from the Āmra grove and proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī, arriving at the abode of Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
At that time, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:

"Now Mañjuśrī has come with this great assembly to inquire after my illness; I should now employ my own supernatural power to empty this room, removing all beds, furnishings, attendants, and gatekeepers, leaving only a single bed upon which I shall manifest lying ill."

At that time, having formed this thought, Vimalakīrti immediately, by means of his great supernormal power, caused the room to become empty and cleared away all its furnishings, leaving only a single couch upon which he appeared to lie ill.

Then Mañjuśrī, together with the great assembly, entered the house; however, they saw only an empty room devoid of any furnishings, attendants, or servants, with the stainless Vimalakīrti alone reclining upon a single bed.
At that time, Vimalakīrti saw Mañjuśrī and called out:
"Welcome! You have come without coming; you are seen without being seen; you are heard without being heard."
Mañjuśrī said: “It is so, householder!
That which has already come cannot come again; that which has already gone cannot go again.”

Why is this so? That which has not yet come cannot be designated as "coming," and that which has already gone cannot be designated as "going. That which has already been seen cannot be seen again, and that which has already been heard cannot be heard again.
Setting this matter aside for a moment,
householder, can your ailment be endured?
Is your life still sustained?
Is his constitution amenable to treatment?
Is his illness curable?
Can this disease be prevented from worsening?
The World-Honored One sends his most earnest greetings to you many times over:
Layman, has this illness of yours improved?
Are your movements and physical strength finding some measure of ease?
"From what does the source of this illness arise?
How long has it been since it was produced, and how should it be extinguished?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"Just as all sentient beings have long been born with ignorance and craving, so too has this illness of mine arisen.
Since the distant beginning of saṃsāra, whenever sentient beings have been ill, I have likewise been ill;
when sentient beings are cured, I am also cured."
Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas depend upon sentient beings who have long been adrift in birth and death; since they depend on birth and death, they are subject to illness.
If sentient beings were to be freed from the suffering of disease, then the bodhisattvas would no longer have any illness.

For example, suppose there is a householder or a wealthy merchant in the world who has an only son. He loves him with the utmost affection, looking upon him with constant joy and never abandoning him for even a moment.
If the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill;
if the son recovers from his illness, the parents also recover.
In this way, the bodhisattva pities all sentient beings as if they were his only child.
When sentient beings are ill, the bodhisattva is also ill;
when the illness of sentient beings is cured, the bodhisattva is also cured.
He asked again,
"From what cause does this illness arise?
[The Buddha replied,] "The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion."
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder,
why is this room entirely empty, and furthermore, why is there no attendant?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"All buddha-fields are likewise entirely empty.
He asked:
"Why is it empty?
Answer: "It is empty by means of emptiness."
He asked again:
"Of what is this emptiness empty?
He replied:
"This emptiness is non-conceptual emptiness.
He asked again:
"Can emptiness be conceptualized?"
He replied:
"This capacity for discrimination is also empty. Why is this so? Because..."
"Emptiness cannot be conceptually differentiated as empty.
He asked again:
"Where should this emptiness be sought?"
He replied:
"This emptiness should be sought within the sixty-two views.
He asked again:
"Where should the sixty-two views be sought?
He replied,
"They should be sought within the liberation of all Buddhas."
He asked again:
"In what should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?
He replied:
"One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding what you asked:
'Why do you have no attendant?'"
"All Māras, adversaries, and various non-Buddhists are my attendants.

Why is this? All Māras and adversaries delight in and praise birth-and-death (saṃsāra), while all non-Buddhists delight in and praise various views; the Bodhisattva does not loathe or abandon them therein. Therefore, Māras, adversaries, and all non-Buddhists are my attendants."
Mañjuśrī said, “Householder,
what are the characteristics of this illness?
He replied:
"My illness has no form or appearance, nor can it be seen.
He asked again:
"Is this illness associated with the body?"
"Is it associated with the mind? He replied,
"My illness is not associated with the body, because the body is detached from characteristics."
It is also associated with the body, because it is like a reflected image;
it is not associated with the mind, because it is detached from the characteristics of the mind;
yet it is also associated with the mind, because it is like a magical illusion.
He asked again:
"Regarding the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element—among these four elements, which element is ill?
He replied:
"The bodies of all sentient beings arise from the four great elements; because they have illness, I am ill.
However, this illness is not identical to the four elements, for it is detached from the nature of the elements."
Vimalakīrti said:
"How should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva so as to cause them to rejoice?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"By demonstrating that the body is impermanent, yet not encouraging weariness with the body; by demonstrating that the body is suffering, yet not encouraging delight in nirvāṇa; by demonstrating that the body is selfless, yet encouraging the maturation of sentient beings; by demonstrating that the body is empty and quiescent, yet not encouraging the cultivation of ultimate extinction; by demonstrating the repentance for past transgressions, yet not saying that transgressions can be transferred; by encouraging one to take pity on all sentient beings through one's own illness so as to eliminate their illnesses; by encouraging mindfulness of the manifold sufferings endured since the beginningless past to benefit sentient beings; by encouraging the recollection of the immeasurable roots of goodness cultivated to practice a pure livelihood; by encouraging the absence of fear and the cultivation of diligent, firm, and courageous effort; and by encouraging the arousal of great vows to become a Great Physician King who cures the physical and mental ailments of all sentient beings so that they may attain eternal peace—thus should a bodhisattva console and encourage a sick bodhisattva, causing them to rejoice."
Mañjuśrī asked,
"How does a sick bodhisattva discipline his mind?
Vimalakīrti replied:
“A sick bodhisattva should form this thought:

‘This illness of mine now arises from karma produced by afflictions of false imagination, inversion, and discrimination since beginningless time. Within this body, there is not a single dharma that is real; who is there that can obtain and receive this illness?’”
Why is this so? The four great elements combine to form what is conventionally designated as a "body"; within these elements there is no master, and the body likewise has no self.
When this illness arises, it necessarily stems from grasping at a self; therefore, one should not falsely give rise to the attachment of a self therein.

When one realizes that this attachment is the root of all illness, for this reason one should eliminate the notion of a "self" regarding all sentient beings and abide in the notion of phenomena (*dharma*).
One should reflect thus:

"This body is formed through the combination of various factors and undergoes the cycle of arising and ceasing; its arising is merely the arising of phenomena, and its ceasing is merely the ceasing of phenomena."

"In this way, all phenomena continue in succession one after another, mutually unaware of each other, and ultimately devoid of thought; when arising, they do not say 'I arise,' and when ceasing, they do not say 'I cease.'"
“A sick bodhisattva should correctly understand this notion of dharmas:
‘This notion of dharmas of mine is itself a perversion.
Indeed, the notion of dharmas is a great affliction; I should eliminate it, and I should also eliminate such a great affliction for all sentient beings.”
How can such a great affliction be eliminated?
It is by eliminating the grasping at "I" and "mine.
How can the grasping at "I" and "mine" be eliminated?
It refers to being free from two things.
What is meant by being free from two things?
It means that internal phenomena and external phenomena ultimately do not function.
What are the two dharmas that ultimately do not function?
They are observing equality as being without movement, without fluctuation, and without anything to be observed.
What is equality?
This means that both "I" and "nirvāṇa" are equally equal.
Why is this? Because the nature of both is empty.
Since these two do not exist, what further could be empty?
It is merely by way of provisional names that they are said to be empty.
Once one has seen that these two are unreal and perceives their equality, no other ailment remains, except for the ailment of emptiness itself.
One should contemplate in this way: even the sickness of emptiness is empty. Why is this?
Because such a sickness of emptiness is ultimately empty.

A sick bodhisattva should experience all sensations while remaining without any subjective grasping. If they have not yet attained perfection in the Buddha-dharma, they should not extinguish sensation to achieve some realization; rather, they should remain detached from both the subject that experiences and the phenomena that are experienced.
"If suffering touches my body, I should take pity on all sentient beings in the miserable realms and, giving rise to great compassion, eliminate their manifold sufferings.
A bodhisattva who is ill should think:
"Having already removed my own illness, I shall also remove the illnesses of all sentient beings."

"In this way, when removing the illnesses of oneself and others, there is not the slightest dharma that can be removed; one should correctly observe the causes and conditions from which the illness arises, swiftly cause it to be extinguished, and preach the True Dharma for them."
What are the causes and conditions of illness?
They are said to be objective referents of mental activity.
All that possesses objective referents in mental activity are causes of illness, because those who possess such objective referents all have illness.
What is its object of focus?
It is said to take the three realms as its object.
How should one understand such an object of focus?
This means correctly realizing that this which possesses objective referents is entirely unapprehendable; if there is nothing apprehended, then there are no objective referents.
How does one sever objective referents?
It means not taking the two views as objects.
What are these two views?
They are the internal view and the external view.

If there are no two views, then there is nothing to be apprehended. Since there is nothing to be apprehended, the movement of mental objects is completely severed. Because the movement of mental objects is severed, there is no illness. If one is oneself without illness, one is able to sever and extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
A sick bodhisattva should discipline his mind in this way:
'Only the bodhi of a bodhisattva can sever all the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death.'"
If it were not so, that which one has diligently cultivated would be in vain. Why is this?
It is, for example, like a person who is called brave and heroic only when they can overcome their enemies; [if they cannot, their prowess is meaningless].
If one can thus forever sever all suffering of old age, sickness, and death, one is called a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
a sick bodhisattva should observe themselves as follows:
Just as this illness of mine is neither real nor existent, so too all illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent.

When contemplating in this way, one should not give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings with a mind entangled by craving and views; rather, one should give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings solely for the purpose of severing adventitious afflictions.
Why is this so? If a bodhisattva, with a mind entangled by craving and views, gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings, they will experience weariness and exhaustion within saṃsāra;
however, if they give rise to great compassion for sentient beings in order to eliminate adventitious afflictions, they will have no weariness or exhaustion within saṃsāra.
In this way, the bodhisattva remains within the cycle of birth and death for the sake of all sentient beings without becoming weary; their mind is not entangled by craving or views.
Because their mind is not entangled by craving or views, they are not bound by birth and death;
because they are not bound by birth and death, they attain liberation.

Because one has attained liberation from birth and death, one possesses the power to proclaim the sublime Dharma, enabling all sentient beings to distance themselves from bondage and realize liberation.
Based on this underlying intention, the World-Honored One said:
"It is impossible for one who is themselves bound to be able to untie the bonds of others;
it is possible for one who has themselves untied their bonds to be able to untie the bonds of others."
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should seek liberation and be free from all fetters.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
what is called the 'fetter' of a bodhisattva?"
What is called the liberation of a bodhisattva?

If bodhisattvas relish and become attached to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) they have cultivated, this is called the bondage of a bodhisattva. If bodhisattvas, by means of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), embrace all forms of existence without any attachment, this is called the liberation of a bodhisattva.
If one lacks skillful means while embracing sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called bondage; if one possesses skillful means while embracing sublime wisdom, it is called liberation.
"What is it that constitutes a bodhisattva’s lack of skillful means in properly embracing sublime wisdom, such that it is called a 'bondage'?

It is when bodhisattvas discipline themselves through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet do not adorn their bodies with the marks and signs, nor purify buddha-fields, nor bring sentient beings to maturity. This lack of skillful means in properly embracing sublime wisdom by these bodhisattvas is called a 'bondage'."
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing skillful means that effectively embraces sublime wisdom, which is called liberation?

It refers to those bodhisattvas who, using the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness to discipline their minds, observe all phenomena—both with signs and without signs—and cultivate them until they realize them through direct realization; furthermore, they adorn their bodies with the primary and secondary marks, purify buddha-fields, and bring sentient beings to maturity. These bodhisattvas, possessing skillful means that effectively embrace sublime wisdom, are said to have attained liberation.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s lack of skillful means in properly embracing sublime wisdom being called 'bondage'?
