It refers to those bodhisattvas who abide in various views, and while under the influence of all afflictions, fetters, and latent tendencies, they cultivate the roots of goodness without dedicating them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment, giving rise to deep attachment. These bodhisattvas, lacking skillful means to properly embrace sublime wisdom, are said to be in bondage."
What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing skillful means that effectively embraces sublime wisdom, which is called liberation?

It refers to those bodhisattvas who, having distanced themselves from all views, all afflictions, fetters, and latent tendencies, cultivate the roots of goodness and are able to dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment without giving rise to attachment; these bodhisattvas, possessing skillful means that effectively embrace sublime wisdom, are said to have attained liberation.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
A bodhisattva who is ill should contemplate that both the body and the illness are entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Although the body is ill and one remains within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit sentient beings without ever becoming weary, this is called skillful means (*upāya*)."

Furthermore, to contemplate that the body, the mind, and all illnesses are mutually dependent, undergoing a beginningless cycle of arising and ceasing without interruption—neither new nor old—is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Not seeking the ultimate extinction of the body, the mind, and all illnesses is called skillful means (*upāya*).
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
A bodhisattva who is ill should discipline his mind in this way: he should not dwell upon a mind that is either disciplined or undisciplined."
Why is this so? To abide in an undisciplined mind is the dharma of the foolish and ordinary; to abide in a disciplined mind is the dharma of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, the bodhisattva does not abide in either of these two extremes; this is what is called the conduct of a bodhisattva.
"If there is a sphere that is neither the sphere of ordinary beings nor the sphere of noble ones, this is called the sphere of the bodhisattva;
if there is a sphere where one observes the sphere of birth and death yet remains free from all afflictions, this is called the sphere of the bodhisattva;
if there is a sphere where one observes the sphere of nirvāṇa yet does not abide in ultimate quiescence, this is called the sphere of the bodhisattva."
If one manifests the activities of the four māras while transcending all activities of the māras, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one seeks the practice of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) without realizing that knowledge at an improper time, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one seeks the practice of the sublime wisdom of the four truths (catuḥsatya-prajñā) without realizing those truths at an improper time, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
If one correctly observes the sphere of internal realization yet intentionally embraces the sphere of saṃsāra, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;
if one practices the sphere of all dependent origination while being able to remain far removed from the sphere of dogmatic views, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;

if one practices the sphere of the mutual disassociation of the phenomena of all sentient beings while remaining free from the sphere of afflictive latent tendencies, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
If one correctly observes the sphere of non-arising without falling into the sphere of the śrāvaka’s fixed nature, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;
if one encompasses the sphere of practice of all sentient beings without the sphere of latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;
if one correctly delights in the sphere of seclusion without seeking the sphere of the total extinction of body and mind, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
If one delights in observing the conduct of the three realms without disrupting the conduct of the dharma-realm, this is called the conduct of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in observing the conduct of emptiness while seeking the conduct of all meritorious qualities, this is called the conduct of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in observing the conduct of signlessness while seeking the conduct of liberating sentient beings, this is called the conduct of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in observing the sphere of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) while being able to manifest the sphere of the realms of existence (*gati*), this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in traversing the sphere of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) while constantly initiating all roots of goodness without cessation, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in traversing the sphere of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) while not failing to reach the shore of excellence regarding the wisdom that understands the mental activities of all sentient beings, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in the practice of the immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, yet does not seek birth in the Brahma world, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in traversing the practice of the six supernormal powers, yet does not proceed toward the realization of the exhaustion of outflows, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in establishing the practice of all dharmas, yet does not take as an object of focus the practice of false paths, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in observing the sphere of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) without giving rise to the sphere of the various outflows (*āsrava*), this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in observing the sphere of non-obstruction without seeking the sphere of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in observing the spheres of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*) while being able to avoid taking birth through the power of those concentrations, this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in traversing the practice of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) but does not delight in seeking the practice of seclusion regarding body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in traversing the practice of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) but does not perceive the two types of practice—wholesome and unwholesome—this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in traversing the practice of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) yet possesses the effortless, sovereign mastery of manifesting psychic powers, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in traversing the domain of the five faculties while practicing the sublime wisdom that does not discriminate between the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one delights in establishing the practice of the five powers while seeking the practice of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in establishing the practice of the perfection of the seven factors of enlightenment while not seeking the skillful means of the sublime wisdom that distinguishes the various aspects of the Buddha-dharma, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in establishing the practice of the perfection of the eight branches of the noble path, yet does not turn away from the practice of the wrong paths, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;
if one seeks the practice of the provisions for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, yet does not fall into the practice of ultimate quiescence, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in observing the practice of all phenomena as being without the marks of arising or ceasing, yet adorns the body with the primary and secondary marks and accomplishes various Buddha-activities, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in manifesting the conduct and deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet does not abandon the practice of contemplating all Buddha-dharmas, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one accords with the ultimate purity of all phenomena, their eternally quiescent intrinsic nature, and the practice of sublime concentration, yet does not fail to accord with the various modes of conduct and deportment that accord with the diverse inclinations of all sentient beings, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva;

if one delights in observing that all buddha-fields are empty and quiescent by nature, without formation or destruction, and acts as space acts, yet does not fail to manifest various merits, adorn buddha-fields, and bring benefit to all sentient beings, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.

If one delights in manifesting all Buddha-dharmas, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering great parinirvāṇa as the sphere of the Buddha’s activities, yet does not fail to practice the various spheres of the bodhisattva practices, this is called the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.

When this account of the marvelous deeds performed by all bodhisattvas was spoken, eight hundred million devaputras among the assembly led by Mañjuśrī heard the Dharma taught and all resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Chapter Six: The Inconceivable. In the sixth chapter, "The Inconceivable," of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Śāriputra, seeing that there were no seats within this room, had this thought to himself:
"Where shall these bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas sit?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra’s mind, spoke to him:
“Indeed, Śāriputra! Have you come for the sake of the Dharma?”
"Are you seeking a bed and seat?
Śāriputra replied,
"I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of a bed and seat."
Vimalakīrti said: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Dharma disregard even their own bodies and lives, let alone a seat."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Those who seek the Dharma do not seek the aggregate of form, nor even the aggregate of consciousness; those who seek the Dharma do not seek the eye-element, nor even the mind-consciousness-element; those who seek the Dharma do not seek the eye-base, nor even the dharma-base; those who seek the Dharma do not seek the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Those who seek the Dharma do not seek attachment to the Buddha, nor attachment to the Dharma or the Saṅgha. Those who seek the Dharma do not seek the knowledge of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the realization of its cessation, or the cultivation of the path."
Why is this so? Because the Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To think, "I shall know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path," is itself conceptual proliferation; it is not what is meant by seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Dharma do not seek arising, nor do they seek cessation. Why is this? "
The Dharma is named tranquility and proximate tranquility; if one practices arising and ceasing, this is seeking arising and ceasing, not seeking the Dharma, nor seeking detachment.
Those who seek the Dharma do not seek defiled attachment.

Why is this so? Because the Dharma is without defilement and is free from all defilements; if one has even the slightest defilement regarding any phenomena, up to and including nirvāṇa, that is seeking defilement, not seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, those who seek the Dharma do not seek after objective realms. Why is this? Because..."
The Dharma is not an objective realm.
To enumerate all objective realms and spheres of activity is to seek after objects; it is not called seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Dharma do not seek taking or abandoning.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is without taking or abandoning.
If one seeks the dharma of grasping and abandoning, that is not called seeking the dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those who seek the dharma do not seek to amass or store it away.
Why is this? Because the Dharma has no concealment.
If one delights in concealment, that is a pursuit of concealment; it is not called seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Dharma do not seek the characteristics of the Dharma. Why is this? "
The Dharma is called signless.
If one follows after signs with consciousness, that is seeking signs, not seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Those who seek the Dharma do not abide in a shared dharma. Why is this?
Because the Dharma has no place of abiding.
If one abides in accordance with the Dharma, that is seeking to abide, not seeking the Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those who seek the Dharma do not seek seeing, hearing, or cognitive awareness.
Why is this? Because the Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.
If one practices seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, this is a pursuit of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not called seeking the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, those who seek the Dharma do not seek the conditioned. Why is this? Because..."
The Dharma is called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), being free from the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one practices the conditioned, this is seeking the conditioned;
it is not called seeking the Dharma. Therefore, Śāriputra!
"If you wish to seek the Dharma, you should not seek anything within all dharmas.
When this teaching was spoken, five hundred devaputras became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all dharmas.

At that time, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous one, you have traveled through immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; in which Buddha-field is there a most excellent, sublime, and perfect Lion Throne endowed with all virtues?"
Mañjuśrī replied:

“To the east, passing from here through as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha-field named Parvata-dhvaja. In that land, the Tathāgata is named Parvata-pradīpa-rāja; he currently dwells there, living in peace and maintaining his teaching.”
That Buddha’s body was eighty-four billion *yojana*s in height, and his lion throne was sixty-eight billion *yojana*s in height;
those bodhisattvas’ bodies were forty-two billion *yojana*s in height, and their lion thrones were thirty-four billion *yojana*s in height.
"Householder, you should know that the lion-thrones of the Tathāgatas in those lands are most exquisite and endowed with every merit.
At that time, Vimalakīrti collected his thoughts, entered meditative concentration, and manifested such sovereign supernormal powers.

Immediately, thirty-two billion great lion thrones—tall, broad, magnificent, pure, and most delightful—sent by the Buddha Mountain-Lamp-King from the Eastern world-system Mountain-Banner, arrived through the air and entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
These bodhisattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and the sons of the gods, had never seen such things before, nor had they ever heard of them previously.

The chamber suddenly became vast, expansive, and pure, fully accommodating thirty-two billion lion thrones without any mutual obstruction. Within it, the Great City of Vaiśālī, Jambudvīpa, the four great continents, and all other worlds—including cities, villages, territories, royal capitals, and the palaces inhabited by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others—were all visible exactly as they were, without any crowding and without any difference between before and after.
Then Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī, "Please take your seat upon the lion throne.
Together with all the bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas, you may sit according to the arrangements made; I shall transform my own body to match the scale of the lion throne."
Those great bodhisattvas who had attained supernormal powers each transformed their bodies to the size of forty-two billion yojanas and ascended the lion thrones, sitting with dignified grace.

None of those newly initiated bodhisattvas were able to ascend the lion thrones; however, at that time, Vimalakīrti expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, causing them all to attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Thereupon, by means of their supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), each transformed themselves into a body forty-two billion *yojanas* in height and ascended the lion thrones, sitting there with majestic dignity.
Among them, there were also many great śrāvakas who were all unable to ascend the lion-thrones.
Then, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Why do you not ascend this seat?
Śāriputra replied, "This seat is high and broad; I am unable to ascend it."
Vimalakīrti said, “Indeed,
Śāriputra! You should pay homage to the Buddha King Mountain Lamp and request that he bestow his supernatural power, for only then will you be able to sit.”

Then the great śrāvakas all immediately paid homage to the Buddha Mountain-Lamp King, requesting that he empower them with his spiritual power; thereupon, they were able to ascend the lion throne and sit upright and majestically.
Śāriputra said:
"How extraordinary, householder!

That such a small room can accommodate so many hundreds of thousands of tall, wide, magnificent, and pure lion-thrones without any obstruction, and that the great city of Vaiśālī, Jambudvīpa, the four continents, and all other worlds—including their cities, villages, kingdoms, royal capitals, and the palaces of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others—are not at all cramped, but are seen exactly as they were before, without any difference."
Vimalakīrti said: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as non-regressive Bodhisattvas, possess a liberation called 'Inconceivable.'"

If a bodhisattva dwelling in such inconceivable liberation takes the King of Mountains, Sumeru, which is so high and vast, and by means of their supernormal power places it within a mustard seed, they cause neither the dimensions of the mustard seed to increase nor the dimensions of the King of Mountains Sumeru to decrease.

Although he manifests such supernatural powers and activities, he does not allow those in the realms of the Four Great Kings or the Thirty-three Gods to know or see where we go or enter; he allows only those remaining who witness his miraculous power and are thereby tamed to perceive the Mount Sumeru entering into a mustard seed.

In this way, the inconceivable realm of liberation entered by a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation through the power of skillful means and wisdom is not to be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva dwelling in such inconceivable liberation can, by means of their supernormal power, place the four great oceans—so deep and vast—within a single pore, yet cause neither the dimensions of the pore to increase nor the dimensions of the four great oceans to decrease."

Although he manifested such supernatural powers and activities, he did not allow those nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others to know or see where we were going or entering; nor did he cause any distress, fear, or harm to the fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and other various species of aquatic life, or to any sentient beings such as the nāga deities. He allowed only those remaining who witnessed his supernormal power and were thereby tamed to perceive these four great oceans entering into a single pore.

In this way, the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation is not to be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva who dwells in such inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernatural power and skillful means, take up this great trichiliocosm—vast in its dimensions—and place it within his right palm; then, spinning it as rapidly as a potter’s wheel, he casts it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, and subsequently brings it back and restores it to its original place, without causing the world to increase or decrease in size."

Although they manifest such miraculous powers and activities, they do not cause the sentient beings dwelling there to perceive where we go or from whence we return; they do not give rise in them even the thought of coming and going, nor do they cause them any affliction or harm. Rather, they cause only those others who witness these miraculous powers and are thereby tamed to perceive that the world comes and goes.

In this way, the inconceivable realm of liberation entered by a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation through the power of skillful means and wisdom is not to be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva who dwells in such inconceivable liberation should find that certain sentient beings are to be tamed by seeing the continuity of birth and death for a long duration, or that other sentient beings are to be tamed by seeing the continuity of birth and death for a short duration, they can, through their supernormal powers, act according to what is appropriate for each: they may extend seven days to constitute one kalpa so that those sentient beings perceive it as having passed one kalpa, or they may condense one kalpa to constitute seven days so that those sentient beings perceive it as having passed seven days, thereby taming them each according to what they see."

Although he manifests such miraculous powers and functions, he does not cause those sentient beings being converted to perceive the lengthening or shortening of time; rather, he causes only those others who witness his miraculous power and are thereby tamed to perceive that lengthening and shortening.

In this way, the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation is not to be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva who dwells in such inconceivable liberation can, by means of their supernormal power, gather all the Buddha-lands adorned with the pure merits of all Buddhas and place them within a single buddha-field to show them to all sentient beings."

Furthermore, by means of their supernormal power, they take all sentient beings of a single buddha-field and place them upon their right palms; then, traveling through the ten directions by the power of mental velocity, they universally manifest all the buddha-fields.
Although they reach all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, they remain in a single Buddha-field without ever shifting.

Furthermore, by their supernormal powers, they manifest from a single pore all manner of supreme and exquisite offerings, traveling throughout all worlds in the ten directions to make offerings to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, by means of his supernormal power, he universally manifests within a single pore all the forms and images of the suns, moons, and stars existing in all worlds throughout the ten directions.

Moreover, by means of his supernormal power, he can even inhale the great wind-circles and other elements of all worlds throughout the ten directions into his mouth without his body being harmed; yet, although the grasses, trees, and forests of all worlds encounter this wind, they remain entirely unmoved.

Furthermore, by means of his supernormal power, he can take all the fires that consume the Buddha-lands throughout the worlds of the ten directions at the end of an eon and place them entirely within his abdomen; although the intensity of these fires blazes without ceasing, they cause him no harm whatsoever.

Furthermore, by means of his supernormal power, he passes beyond immeasurable *koṭi* of *Gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-worlds in the direction below, lifts up a single Buddha-field, and hurls it into a Buddha-field beyond *koṭi* of *Gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-worlds in the direction above; just as one might lift a small jujube leaf with the point of a needle and hurl it to another place without causing it any damage at all.

Although he manifests such miraculous powers and activities, those who lack the karmic affinity neither see nor know them; yet he ultimately causes no harm or affliction to any sentient beings, but rather ensures that all who behold his miraculous power and are thereby tamed do indeed perceive these events.

In this way, the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva dwelling in inconceivable liberation is not to be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva who dwells in such inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal power, manifest the various forms and images of a Buddha’s body; or manifest the various forms and images of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; or manifest the various forms and images of bodhisattvas—fully adorned with all the primary marks and secondary signs—or further manifest the various forms and images of all sentient beings, such as Brahmā kings, Śakra, the four great heavenly kings, and universal monarchs."

Or, by means of supernormal power, they transform sentient beings so that they appear in various forms, such as the bodies of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors (lokapālas), or universal monarchs (cakravartin).

Or, by means of supernatural power, he transforms all the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior voices of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, making them all into the Buddha’s voice, the most sublime and subtle. From this Buddha-voice, there issue forth various verbal expressions such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, ultimate nirvāṇa, and the meaning of tranquility; even the sounds of the Dharma teachings of all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas emerge from within it. Furthermore, all the names, phrases, syllables, and vocal distinctions used by the Buddhas of the ten directions when teaching the Dharma emerge from such a Buddha-voice, universally enabling all sentient beings to hear them and bringing them all to subdual according to their respective vehicles.

Or, by means of supernormal power, throughout the ten directions, in accordance with the various differences in the speech and sounds of sentient beings, they produce diverse sounds as appropriate to each, expounding the sublime Dharma so that all sentient beings may each obtain benefit.
"Indeed, Śāriputra!
I have now briefly explained the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom of a bodhisattva who dwells in such inconceivable liberation."
If I were to explain this in detail, it might take an eon, or more than an eon, or even longer; yet my wisdom and eloquence would never be exhausted.

Just as my wisdom and eloquence are inexhaustible, so too the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom by a bodhisattva dwelling in such inconceivable liberation is inexhaustible, because it is immeasurable.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard this discourse on the inconceivable power of liberation of the bodhisattvas who abide in inconceivable liberation, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"It is as if someone were to display various distinct forms and images before one born blind; yet that blind person would be entirely unable to see them."

In this way, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are like those born blind, lacking the eye of excellence; when they hear of the inconceivable power of liberation manifested by a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation, they cannot comprehend even a single such matter.
What wise person—whether man or woman—who hears such an account of the inconceivable power of liberation would not resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
"We are now like scorched and rotten seeds within this Mahāyāna; our roots are forever severed. What more can we do?
All of us Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, upon hearing such accounts of the inconceivable power of liberation, should all wail and weep until the sound shakes the trichiliocosm."

Upon hearing such accounts of the inconceivable power of liberation and spiritual transformations, all bodhisattvas should rejoice, receive them with reverence, and uphold them, just as a royal prince receives the consecration of his rank and thereby develops the power of firm faith and understanding.

If there is a bodhisattva who hears this teaching on such inconceivable liberation and supernatural power, and develops firm faith and understanding, then all Māras and their hosts will be unable to do anything to that bodhisattva.
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had spoken these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras within the assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then Vimalakīrti spoke to the venerable Kāśyapa:

"The countless and infinite world-systems in the ten directions where there are those who act as Māras are, for the most part, bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who have manifested as Māras through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) for the sake of bringing sentient beings to spiritual maturity."
Mahākāśyapa! All bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and countless worlds of the ten directions— whosoever comes to seek their hands,
feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, blood, flesh, sinews, or bones— [should give them].
All their limbs and bodies, wives and concubines, sons and daughters, slaves and servants, kinsmen and relatives;
villages, cities, towns, districts, royal capitals, and the four great continents;
as well as various royal ranks, wealth, grain, treasures, gold, silver, pearls, coral, conch shells, cowries, and lapis lazuli.
Regarding all such ornaments, dwellings, couches and seats, clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions,
assets, elephants, horses, carriages, large and small ships, weapons, and military hosts—
whosoever thus oppresses a bodhisattva by begging for these things, they are for the most part established in the inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Vimukta, through skillful means, manifested these events to test the bodhisattva,
so as to cause him to realize that his resolve was firm. Why was this?
The great Bodhisattvas, possessing supreme courage and vigor, manifest such difficult-to-accomplish great deeds for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Ordinary persons of inferior capacity lack the power to compel a Bodhisattva to engage in such begging.
“Mahākāśyapa! For example, a firefly can never possess the power to obscure the orb of the sun.
In the same way, ordinary persons and those of inferior status have no further power to compel a bodhisattva to beg for this.”

Mahākāśyapa! For example, when a dragon-elephant displays its majesty in battle, it is not something a donkey can endure; only a dragon-elephant can engage in such combat with another dragon-elephant.

In this way, ordinary beings and those in inferior states lack the power to coerce a bodhisattva; only a bodhisattva can mutually coerce another bodhisattva. This is called the inconceivable realm of liberation entered through the power of skillful means and wisdom of a bodhisattva who dwells in inconceivable liberation.
When this Dharma was being taught, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained entry into the inconceivable realm of liberation through the power of skillful means and wisdom of the bodhisattvas.
The Sutra Spoken by Vimalakīrti, Scroll Three;
The Sutra Spoken by Vimalakīrti, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings At that time,
Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti,
“How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?”
Vimalakīrti said:
“Just as a master of illusions observes his own illusory creations,
so too should a bodhisattva correctly observe all sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
It is as if a wise person were to contemplate the moon in water, contemplate an image in a mirror, contemplate the water of a mirage, contemplate the echo of a shout,
contemplate the cloud-castles and towers in the sky, or contemplate the mass of foam upon the water— all of which have no prior [reality]."
At that time, one contemplates the bubbles on water as they arise and perish; one contemplates the core of a plantain tree for its solidity;
one contemplates a fifth great element, a sixth aggregate, a seventh sense-faculty, the thirteen bases, and the nineteen elements;
one contemplates the various forms and images within the formless realm; and one contemplates what can emerge from a scorched and rotten seed.
Contemplating garments made from ivory stalks or tortoise hair; contemplating the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by those who have died young;

contemplating the arising of the conceptual view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); contemplating the taking of a third existence by one who has attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*);
contemplating the entry into the mother’s womb by one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*); and contemplating the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion in an Arhat.

To contemplate the stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, and harmful intent of a bodhisattva who has attained patient acceptance; to contemplate the continuity of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) in all Tathāgatas;
to contemplate those born blind beholding various forms; to contemplate the inhalation and exhalation of breath in one abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
to contemplate the tracks of birds in the midst of empty space; and to contemplate the functional potency of the sexual organs of a paṇḍaka.
To contemplate the activities of a stone child; to contemplate the arising of various fetters in those emanated by a Buddha;
to contemplate afflictions that are ultimately non-arising; to contemplate what is seen in a dream after waking from it; to contemplate a fire that does not arise yet performs the act of burning;
and to contemplate the continuity of subsequent existence in an Arhat.
In this way, a bodhisattva should correctly observe all sentient beings. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are fundamentally empty, being in truth without self and without sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī said:
"If bodhisattvas observe all sentient beings in this manner, how do they cultivate great loving-kindness toward them?
Vimalakīrti replied:
“Having observed sentient beings in this way, the bodhisattva reflects:
‘I shall explain such a Dharma to all sentient beings so that they may understand it.’”
This is called truly cultivating great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which brings ultimate peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
In this way, the bodhisattva cultivates the loving-kindness of cessation (*śānti-maitrī*) because they are free from all grasping;
they cultivate the loving-kindness of non-fever (*an-uṣṇa-maitrī*) because they are detached from afflictions (*kleśa*).
One cultivates the compassion of suchness, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time;
one cultivates the compassion of non-opposition, because it is without origination;
one cultivates non-dual compassion, because it is free from the internal and external.
He cultivates indestructible loving-kindness because he abides in it ultimately;
he cultivates firm loving-kindness because his superior intention is like a vajra;
he cultivates pure loving-kindness because its intrinsic nature is pure.
One cultivates the compassion of equanimity, because it is equal to empty space;
one cultivates the compassion of an arhat, because it forever destroys the thieves of the fetters;
one cultivates the compassion of a pratyekabuddha, because it does not depend upon teachers or patrons.
One cultivates the compassion of a bodhisattva because of never ceasing to bring sentient beings to maturity;
one cultivates the compassion of a Tathāgata because of awakening to the true suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena;
one cultivates the compassion of a Buddha because of awakening all sentient beings from their sleep and dreams.
One cultivates spontaneous compassion, because it spontaneously awakens to the nature of all phenomena;
one cultivates the compassion of enlightenment, because it is of a single flavor;
one cultivates impartial compassion, because attachment and aversion have been severed.
One cultivates the compassion of great pity because it reveals the Mahāyāna;
one cultivates the compassion free from contention because it contemplates non-self;
one cultivates the compassion free from weariness because it contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
One cultivates the compassion of the gift of Dharma because it is free from the conceit of being a teacher;
one cultivates the compassion of pure ethical discipline because it brings to maturity those sentient beings who have transgressed the precepts;
one cultivates the compassion of forbearance because it protects oneself and others according to their needs so that neither is harmed.
One cultivates the loving-kindness of diligence for the sake of bearing the burden of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
one cultivates the loving-kindness of meditative concentration because it is free from the savoring of attachment;
and one cultivates the loving-kindness of wisdom because of the direct knowledge of phenomena at all times.
They cultivate the compassion of skillful means, because it is universally manifested through all gateways;
they cultivate the compassion of sublime vows, because it is elicited by immeasurable great vows;
they cultivate the compassion of great power, because it is able to accomplish all vast undertakings.
One cultivates the compassion of *jñāna* because of thoroughly understanding the nature and characteristics of all phenomena;
one cultivates the compassion of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) because of not destroying the nature and characteristics of all phenomena;
one cultivates the compassion of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) because of skillfully gathering in and benefiting all sentient beings.
One cultivates unattached loving-kindness because it is free from defilement;
one cultivates non-deceptive loving-kindness because the underlying intention is pure;
one cultivates non-crooked loving-kindness because the application is pure.
One cultivates the compassion of non-deception, because it is not false or artificial;
one cultivates the compassion of the profound mind, because it is free from defilement;
one cultivates the compassion of peace and happiness, because it establishes the matters of peace and happiness for all Buddhas.
"O Mañjuśrī! This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of great loving-kindness. Mañjuśrī said:
“How does a bodhisattva cultivate great compassion?
Vimalakīrti replied,

“To relinquish all that has been performed and accumulated as roots of goodness, and to give them to all sentient beings without any stinginess— this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of great compassion.”
Mañjuśrī asked,
"How does a bodhisattva cultivate great joy?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"To feel joy and have no regrets while performing beneficial deeds for all sentient beings—this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of great sympathetic joy (muditā).
Mañjuśrī asked: "How does a bodhisattva cultivate great equanimity (upekṣā)?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"To benefit others with equanimity, without expecting a reward—this is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of great relinquishment. Mañjuśrī said:
"If bodhisattvas fear birth and death, upon what should they rely?
Vimalakīrti replied,
"If bodhisattvas fear birth and death, they should always correctly rely and abide in the Great Self (mahātman) of the Buddhas."
He asked again:
“If a bodhisattva wishes to abide in the Great Self, how should they abide?
He replied:
"One who wishes to abide in the Great Self should abide in the equal liberation of all sentient beings.
He asked again:
"If one wishes to bring about the liberation of all sentient beings, what must be eliminated?"
He replied,
"I wish to bring all sentient beings to liberation and eliminate their afflictions.
He asked again:
"If one wishes to eliminate the afflictions of all sentient beings, what should one cultivate?
He replied:
"If one wishes to eliminate the afflictions of all sentient beings, one should cultivate the mental attention of investigating according to reality."
He asked again:
"If one wishes to cultivate the mental attention of thorough investigation according to reality, how should one cultivate it?
He replied:
"If one wishes to cultivate the mental attention of investigating according to reality, one should cultivate the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena.
He asked again:
"Which phenomena do not arise?"
"What dharma does not cease?
He replied:
"The unwholesome does not arise; wholesome dharmas do not cease."
He asked again:
"What is the root of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas?
He replied:
"The body is the foundation.
He asked again,
"What is the foundation of the body?"
He replied,
“Desire and greed are the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of sensual desire?
He replied:
"False conceptualization is its root."
He asked again:
"What is the root of false discrimination?
He replied:
"Inverted perception is the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of inverted perception?"
He replied,
"Non-abiding is the foundation. Mañjuśrī said:
"Thus, if there is no abiding, what could serve as its basis?
Vimalakīrti replied,
"This question is illogical."
Why is this so? That which is non-abiding has no fundamental basis and nothing upon which it rests.
Because it has no fundamental basis and nothing upon which it rests, it is able to establish all dharmas.

At that time, there was a goddess who had long resided within the chamber of Vimalakīrti. Having seen these great beings and heard the Dharma they preached, she experienced something unprecedented; filled with leaping joy and delight, she manifested her form and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the bodhisattvas and the assembly of great śrāvakas.
At that time, the celestial flowers reached the bodies of the Bodhisattvas and immediately fell away, but upon reaching the Great Śrāvakas, they adhered and did not fall.
Then the assembly of Śrāvakas each desired to remove the flowers; they exerted all their supernatural powers, yet none were able to remove them.
At that time, the goddess asked the Venerable Śāriputra,
"For what reason do you remove these flowers?
Śāriputra replied:
"The flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; that is why I have removed them.
The goddess said, "Stop! Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma."
Why is this? These flowers are in accordance with the Dharma, whereas you venerable ones yourselves are not in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this?
The flower has no conceptualization (*vikalpa*) nor discursive differentiation (*parikalpa*); it is only the Venerable Ones who themselves possess conceptualization and discursive differentiation.
Within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, if those who have gone forth possess conceptualization and discursive differentiation, they are not in accordance with the Dharma;
if they are without conceptualization and without discursive differentiation, they are in accordance with the Dharma.
"Consider this, Śāriputra!

Observe that those bodhisattvas upon whom the flowers do not adhere have all permanently severed all conceptualization and discursive differentiation; observe that those śrāvakas to whose bodies the flowers adhere have all failed to sever all conceptualization and discursive differentiation."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Just as when a person is afraid, non-human beings find an opportunity;
if one has no fear, no non-human being can find an opportunity."
If one fears birth-and-death, karma, and afflictions, then form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth will find their opportunity;
if one does not fear birth-and-death, karma, and afflictions, then the worldly form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth will find no opportunity.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If the habitual tendencies of afflictions have not been permanently severed, the flowers will adhere to their bodies;
if the habitual tendencies of afflictions have already been permanently severed, the flowers will not adhere.
Śāriputra asked, “Heavenly maiden,
how long has it been since you entered this room?
The goddess replied:
"I have been dwelling in this chamber as if in the liberation in which Śāriputra dwells. Śāriputra said,
"Has the goddess been dwelling in this chamber for such a long time?"
The goddess spoke again:
"How long has it been since you attained the liberation in which you abide?
At that time, Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The goddess said:
"Venerable One, you are a great śrāvaka, endowed with great wisdom and eloquence; yet, upon receiving this minor question, you remain silent and do not answer.
Śāriputra replied:
"Furthermore, liberation is free from all names and expressions; as for me, what could I possibly say regarding this?
The deva said, "The very words spoken are all the characteristics of liberation."
Why is this so? This liberation cannot be found within, nor without, nor in between the two;
likewise, words and letters cannot be found within, nor without, nor in between the two.
Therefore, there is no liberation apart from words.
Why is this? Because liberation is equal in nature to all phenomena.
Śāriputra said:
"Is it not by being free from greed, hatred, and delusion that one attains liberation?
The goddess replied:
The Buddha taught those with overweening pride that liberation consists in being free from all greed, hatred, and delusion;
however, for those who have distanced themselves from overweening pride, he taught that the very nature of all greed, hatred, and delusion is itself liberation.
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, O goddess!
What realization have you attained such that your wisdom and eloquence are like this?"
The deva said:
"I have now nothing attained and nothing realized; such is my wisdom and eloquence.
If one were to say that I have now something attained or something realized, they would be guilty of overweening pride regarding this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya."
Śāriputra asked,
"In which of the three vehicles have you set out?
The goddess replied:
"I am setting out upon all three vehicles.
Śāriputra asked,
"With what underlying intention do you speak thus?"
The deva said:
“Because I constantly proclaim the Mahāyāna so that others may hear it, I am a śrāvaka;
because I have spontaneously and directly awakened to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), I am a pratyekabuddha.”
Because I never abandon great compassion, I am the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
because I transform and deliver those sentient beings who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, I am the śrāvaka.
For the sake of transforming and delivering those sentient beings who seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, I am a Pratyekabuddha;
for the sake of transforming and delivering those sentient beings who seek the Supreme Vehicle, I am the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is as if there were a person who enters a campaka grove; they smell only the fragrance of the campaka flowers, never taking pleasure in smelling the scents of grass, hemp, or the like."

In this way, if anyone dwells in this chamber, they will delight solely in the fragrance of the merits of the Mahāyāna and never take pleasure in the fragrances of the merits of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, because this chamber is constantly perfumed by the sublime fragrance of all the merits of the Buddha-dharma.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All those who enter this chamber—whether they be Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Great Kings, nāgas, yakṣas, or asuras, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans—all do so to behold such a mahāsattva, to draw near, pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the Great Dharma; they all give rise to the mind of great bodhi and depart carrying the wondrous fragrance of the merits of all Buddha-dharmas."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I have dwelt in this room for twelve years, yet I have never heard any discourse associated with the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; I have heard only discourses associated with the Mahāyāna, the practices of the Bodhisattvas, and the inconceivable, sublime Dharma of all Buddhas, characterized by great loving-kindness and great compassion."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
in this room eight extraordinary and sublime phenomena are constantly manifested.
What are these eight?
"Śāriputra, it is thus:

this chamber is constantly pervaded by a golden radiance that shines everywhere, without distinction between day and night; it does not rely on the illumination of the sun or moon for its light. This is the first unprecedented and extraordinary quality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This room is always filled with all kinds of worldly humans and non-humans; once they have entered this room, they cannot be harmed by any afflictions. This is the second unprecedented and extraordinary quality.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This room is never empty of the constant assembly of all the Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Great Kings, as well as the great bodhisattvas from other worlds; this is the third extraordinary and sublime quality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In this room, one constantly hears discourses corresponding to the irreversible wheel of Dharma regarding the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of the bodhisattvas; this is the fourth extraordinary and sublime quality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This chamber constantly produces celestial music, from which emerge immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sounds of the Dharma; this is the fifth unprecedented and extraordinary quality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This room always contains four great treasuries, overflowing with all manner of rare jewels that never run out. They provide for all who are poor, widowed, orphaned, destitute, or begging, fulfilling their every wish without ever being exhausted. This is the sixth extraordinary and sublime quality."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

This room is constantly filled with the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata Amitāyus, the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, the Tathāgata Ratnārcis, the Tathāgata Ratnacandra, the Tathāgata Ratnavyūha, the Tathāgata Ratnasvara, the Tathāgata Siṃhanāda, the Tathāgata Sarvārthasiddha, and such immeasurable Tathāgatas from the ten directions."

If this Great Being should resolve his mind and offer a prayer, they will arrive immediately at that very moment to extensively proclaim all the secret and essential Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas; having finished speaking, they depart. This is the seventh extraordinary and sublime quality.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In this room, the meritorious adornments of all buddha-fields and the exquisite, wondrous decorations of the celestial palaces are constantly manifested; this is the eighth extraordinary and sublime quality."
"Indeed, Śāriputra!

This chamber constantly manifests eight extraordinary and sublime dharmas. Who, having witnessed such inconceivable matters, would again resolve their mind to seek the path of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha?"
Then Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"Why do you not transform this female body?
The goddess replied:
“I have dwelt in this room for twelve years, yet I have been unable to find the nature of a woman anywhere;
what, then, could possibly be transformed? O, Śāriputra!...”
It is like a magician who conjures an illusory woman.
If someone were to ask him,
"Why do you not transform this woman's body?"
“Is this not a correct question?
Śāriputra replied, “No, goddess!”
"Since an illusion is not real, what could possibly be transformed?
The goddess said, "In this way, the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are not real; they are like magical illusions. Why, then, do you ask how one does not transform a female body?"
Immediately, the goddess used her supernormal powers to transform Śāriputra so that he appeared like a goddess, while she transformed herself into the likeness of Śāriputra, and asked him:
"Venerable One!
"How is it that you have not transformed your female body?
At that time, Śāriputra, appearing in the form of a goddess, replied to him, saying,
"I do not know how to transform and eliminate my male body or transform and give rise to a female appearance."
The goddess spoke again:
"Venerable One, if you could transform this female body, then all female bodies could likewise be transformed.
Just as Śāriputra is truly not a woman yet manifests in a female body;"
The bodies of all women are likewise; although they manifest as female bodies, they are in reality not female.
It was with this underlying intention that the World-Honored One said:
"All dharmas are neither male nor female."
When the goddess had finished speaking these words, she withdrew her supernormal power and each returned to their original form. She then asked Śāriputra:
"Venerable One, where is that female body now?"
Śāriputra said:
"Now this female body of mine neither exists nor undergoes transformation.
The goddess said:
“Venerable sir!
Excellent, excellent!
All phenomena are likewise thus: they neither exist nor undergo change.”
"To say that all phenomena are non-abiding and unchanging is the true word of the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"When you pass away from here, where will you be reborn?"
The goddess replied,
“I shall be born in whatever place the Tathāgata’s emanations are to be born.
Śāriputra said:
“The emanations of the Tathāgata neither pass away nor are born.
Why, then, do you speak of a place where they shall be born?
The deva replied:
“Venerable sir!
All phenomena and sentient beings should likewise be understood as neither passing away nor being born.
Why then do you ask me where I shall be reborn?”
Then Śāriputra asked the goddess,
"How long will it be before you realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The goddess replied:

"If Śāriputra were to become a worldling again and possess the qualities of a worldling, my realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening would likewise be as long ago as that. Śāriputra said,
"There is no place and no possibility that I should ever become a worldling again and possess the qualities of a worldling."
The goddess said:
"Venerable One!
I am likewise; there is no place and no position from which I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Why is this? Because unsurpassed bodhi has no place of abiding, therefore there is also no one who realizes bodhi.
Śāriputra said:
“If that is so, why did the Buddha say that Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have realized, are realizing, and will realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The deva replied:
“Venerable One!...”

All these are merely words, conventional designations, and linguistic expressions, spoken of as the Buddhas of the three periods attaining realization; it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present.
Why is this? Because unsurpassed enlightenment transcends the three periods of time.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
"Have you already realized arhatship?
Śāriputra replied, "I have attained what is not attained; I have attained non-attainment."
The deva said:
"Venerable One!
Awakening is likewise: it is realized without being realized, for there is nothing to be realized."
Then Vimalakīrti spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra: "It is so;

this goddess has already made offerings to, drawn near to, and served ninety-two hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas. She is able to sport with supernatural powers and wisdom, her vows are fulfilled, she has attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and she has never again regressed from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. By the power of her original vows, she matures sentient beings wherever it is appropriate, according to her wishes."
Chapter Eight: The Factors of Enlightenment. In the eighth chapter of the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, "The Factors of Enlightenment," Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti:
"How does a bodhisattva reach the ultimate consummation regarding all the Buddha-dharmas?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"If bodhisattvas practice by way of non-approach, they reach the ultimate approach within the Buddha-dharma.
Mañjuśrī asked:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva practicing in the non-gatis?
Vimalakīrti replied, “If a bodhisattva,
even while practicing within the five *anantarya* hells, remains free from malice, affliction, anger, harm, and a poisonous mind;”
Although they may travel through the realm of hell-beings, they remain free from all defilements of affliction;
although they may travel through the realms of animals, they remain free from all darkness of ignorance;
although they may travel through the realm of asuras, they remain free from all arrogance and self-indulgence.
Although they may travel through the realm of King Yama, they accumulate vast stores of merit and wisdom;
although they may travel through the realm of the formless attainments, they do not take delight in or incline toward them;
and although they manifest the conduct of sensual desire, they remain free from all defiled attachments amidst all objects of desire they experience.
Although he manifests the conduct of those who follow the path of hatred, he remains free from all hatred toward the realm of sentient beings and harbors no intent to harm;

although he manifests the conduct of those who follow the path of delusion, he is far removed from all darkness of ignorance regarding all phenomena and disciplines himself through the light of wisdom;
although he manifests the conduct of those who follow the path of stinginess and greed, he is able to relinquish all internal and external things, disregarding even his own body and life.

Although he manifests the conduct of violating the precepts, he is able to establish himself in all forms of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the ascetic virtues (*dhūta-guṇa*), fewness of desires, and contentment, perceiving great terror even in minor transgressions;
although he manifests the conduct of anger and resentment, he is ultimately able to abide in loving-kindness and compassion, his mind free from malice or affliction;
although he manifests the conduct of indolence, he is able to diligently cultivate all roots of goodness, his vigor never faltering.
Although they manifest the practice of wandering through the realms of sensory distraction, they remain ever serene and silent, dwelling peacefully in meditative concentration;

although they manifest the practice of wandering through the realms of faulty wisdom, they skillfully penetrate all mundane and supramundane faith, reaching the ultimate perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*);
although they manifest the practice of wandering through the realms of deceit and guile, they are able to accomplish skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Although he manifests the practice of expedient means through esoteric speech and the course of prideful conduct, he establishes a bridge for deliverance;
although he manifests the practice of all worldly afflictions, his nature is fundamentally pure and ultimately untainted;
although he manifests the course of the various Māras, he personally realizes the wisdom of awakening regarding all Buddha-dharmas and does not rely on external conditions.
Although they manifest the practice of the vehicle of the śrāvakas, they preach the Dharma never heard before for the sake of sentient beings;
although they manifest the practice of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they bring sentient beings to maturity through the accomplishment of great loving-kindness and great compassion;
and although they appear to dwell among those in states of poverty, they possess the jewel-hand from which precious wealth is inexhaustible.
Although he manifests in realms of those with impaired faculties, his body is adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and a wondrous complexion;
although he manifests in the birth-realm of the lowly and base, he is born into the Buddha-family with noble lineage, having accumulated a preeminent store of merit and wisdom;
although he manifests in realms that are frail, inferior, ugly, and loathed by all, he attains a supreme and wondrous Nārāyaṇa body, which all sentient beings constantly delight to behold.
Although he manifests in the realms of old age and sickness, he is ultimately able to eradicate the roots of old age and sickness and transcend all fears of death;
although he manifests in the realm of seeking wealth and status, he frequently cultivates the perception of impermanence and brings all cravings to rest;
although he manifests in the realm of palaces, courtesans, and various amusements, he constantly transcends the mire of desire and cultivates the practice of ultimate detachment.

Although he manifests in the realms of the dull-witted and the ignorant, he is adorned with various forms of talent and eloquence, having attained *dhāraṇī* such that his mindfulness and wisdom are never lost;
although he manifests in the realms of all heterodox paths, he delivers all worlds by means of the true path;
although he manifests in all modes of birth, he has in truth forever severed all rebirth in the realms of existence.
Although they manifest entry into the state of parinirvāṇa, they never abandon the continuity of saṃsāra;

although they manifest the attainment of wondrous bodhi, the turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and entry into the state of nirvāṇa, they nevertheless diligently cultivate all bodhisattva practices in an uninterrupted succession.
"O Mañjuśrī! When a bodhisattva practices in this way within the non-destinies, they are said to have reached the ultimate destination regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī:
“What is called the Tathāgata-lineage?
I pray that you will explain it briefly. Mañjuśrī replied:

"What is called the lineage of all false bodies is the Tathāgata’s lineage; the lineage of all ignorance, existence, and craving is the Tathāgata’s lineage; the lineage of greed, hatred, and delusion is the Tathāgata’s lineage; and the lineage of the four kinds of false inversions is the Tathāgata’s lineage."

In this way, the nature of the five hindrances, the nature of the six sense bases, the nature of the seven stations of consciousness, the nature of the eightfold wrong path, the nature of the nine grounds for resentment, and the nature of the ten unwholesome paths of action—these are the lineage of the Tathāgata.
In brief, the sixty-two views, all afflictions, and the seeds of all evil and unwholesome dharmas constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Vimalakīrti asked,
"With what underlying intention did you speak thus?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"One who has not seen the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and has already entered the stage of the certainty of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) cannot give rise to the mind of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; rather, it is one who dwells amidst conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and afflictions, and has not yet seen the truths (*satya*), who can give rise to the mind of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."
For example, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and water lilies do not grow on high ground or dry land; these four kinds of flowers can only grow in low-lying, damp, and foul mud.

In this way, those of the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have already seen the unconditioned and have entered the stage of the certainty of rightness can never give rise to the mind of omniscience; it is only within the low-lying, damp, and foul mud of the afflictions and conditioned formations that one can give rise to the mind of omniscience, for therein all the Buddha-dharmas grow and flourish.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like planting a seed in mid-air; it will never grow. Only when planted in low-lying, moist soil enriched with manure can it grow."

In this way, those of the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have already seen the unconditioned and have entered the stage of the certainty of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma) are unable to grow all the Buddha-dharmas; yet, even if they give rise to a view of a self as vast as Mount Sumeru, they are able to initiate the vow for great enlightenment (mahābodhicitta), because within that state they can grow all the Buddha-dharmas.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as a person who does not enter the great ocean can never obtain priceless precious jewels such as vaiḍūrya, so too one who does not enter the great ocean of the afflictions of birth and death can never give rise to the priceless jewel of the mind of omniscience."
"Therefore, you should know that the very nature of all afflictions within birth and death is the nature of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"

This is most excellently taught as truthful speech, consistent with reality, sincere, and without discrepancy: that the very nature of all birth-and-death and afflictions is the Tathāgata-nature. Why is this so?

Within the continuum of our minds, the seeds of birth and death have now all been scorched and destroyed; we shall never again be able to give rise to the mind of perfect enlightenment. It would be better for us to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution than to fail to achieve the ultimate liberation of us Arhats.

Why is this? Those who have committed the five kinds of deeds of immediate retribution still possess the power to exhaust those karmic obstacles, to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and to gradually accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas;
we, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, forever lack such capacity, just as one who is missing sense organs is incapable of enjoying the five exquisite sensual pleasures.

In this way, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted have forever severed all fetters; they are thus incapable of further action regarding the Buddha-dharma and no longer aspire to seek the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas.
Therefore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness, whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas can never do so.

Why is this? Because when ordinary beings hear of the merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, they ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels will never be severed; they are able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*), and gradually accomplish all the Buddha-dharmas.

Even if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were to hear an exposition of all the qualities of the Tathāgata—ranging from the powers and fearlessnesses up to all the unique buddha-qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma)—for the rest of their lives, they would ultimately never be able to give rise to the mind of perfect enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhicitta).
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana who asked Vimalakīrti:
"Householder!
Who are all these people—your parents, wife, children, slaves, servants, friends, kinsmen, attendants, elephants, horses, carriages, charioteers, and their like?"
"Where are they all located?
At that time, Vimalakīrti replied to him with these sublime verses:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Skillful Means is their father."
All true guides of the world arise from this.
Taking the wondrous Dharma as their beloved wife, Great compassion as their daughter,
The truth of reality as their son, And the contemplation of emptiness and ultimate meaning as their home—
Afflictions serve as lowly slaves, Servants who turn according to one's will;
The factors of enlightenment are dear friends, By means of which one realizes bodhi.
The six perfections are kinsmen, The four means of integration are courtesans.
The words of the compiled True Dharma serve as exquisite music;
Dhāraṇīs form the groves and gardens, and the Great Dharma becomes the forest trees;
Adorned with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment, They bear the fruits of liberation and wisdom.
The wondrous pond of the eight liberations is filled with the limpid waters of meditative concentration;
the blossoms of the seven purities spread far and wide, washing away all defilements.
With supernormal powers as elephants and horses, and the Mahāyāna as the chariot, [one proceeds].
Taming and governing the bodhicitta, one traverses the paths of the Eightfold Noble Way.
Adorned with the perfection of the primary marks and interspersed with the exquisite secondary signs,
one wears the robes of shame and modesty, and the garlands of sublime resolve.
Possessing the precious wealth of the True Dharma, they provide instruction as a skillful means;
through unerring practice they achieve victory, dedicating it toward Great Enlightenment.
With the four dhyānas as their bed and pure livelihood as their mattress,
Mindfulness and wisdom are ever-awakened; there is no moment when the mind is not in meditative concentration.
Having partaken of the Dharma of immortality, one drinks again of the flavor of liberation;
one bathes in the wondrously pure mind and anoints oneself with the supreme fragrance of the precepts.
Having utterly destroyed the thieves of affliction, Brave and invincible,
he subdues the four Māra-enemies And raises the sublime banner of Bodhi.
Although in truth there is neither arising nor ceasing, He intentionally undergoes rebirth.
They manifest all Buddha-lands, like the sunlight shining everywhere;
taking up every supreme and wondrous offering, they present them to all Tathāgatas,
without making any distinction between the Buddhas and themselves.
Though they know that all Buddha-fields and sentient beings are empty,
they constantly cultivate pure lands, benefiting others without rest or weariness.
Regarding all classes of sentient beings— their forms, sounds, and modes of deportment—
The Bodhisattva Fearless Power can manifest everything in a single instant.
Though he perceives all the activities of Māra, he demonstrates compliance with them;
through ultimate skillful means, all manifested deeds are brought to fulfillment.
Sometimes they manifest their own bodies as subject to old age, sickness,
and death to bring sentient beings to maturity, like playing with illusory phenomena;
sometimes they manifest the arising of the kalpa-fire, wherein heaven and earth are all ablaze.
Sentient beings cling to the notion of permanence; I illuminate them so they may know swift cessation.
When billions of sentient beings from all lands come together to request my presence, I accept their offerings simultaneously, Causing them all to advance toward Bodhi.
Regarding all incantations and arts, as well as books, treatises, and various crafts,
he knows them all to their ultimate limit, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Among all the worldly paths and dharmas, he has gone forth as a renunciant throughout them all.
Acting in accordance with skillful means to benefit sentient beings, they do not fall into various views.
Sometimes they become the sun, the moon, a deva, a Brahmā king, or a lord of the world;
as earth, water, fire, and wind, they bring benefit to the classes of sentient beings.
In eons of pestilence, they manifest as various excellent medicines,
eliminating all suffering from disease and leading beings toward Great Bodhi;
in eons of famine, they manifest as various foods and drinks.
First, one dispels their hunger and thirst, then teaches the Dharma to bring them peace and security;
during the kalpa of weapons, one cultivates the meditative concentration of loving-kindness and compassion,
causing immeasurable sentient beings to rejoice without malice or harm.
Able, amidst great battles and arrays, to manifest as a faction of strength,
going back and forth to bring about reconciliation and harmony, and exhorting others to resolve upon the Bodhicitta.
Throughout the infinite Buddha-fields and the boundless hells, [they act in this way].
He goes to all those places to uproot suffering and bring about peace and happiness.
To all those in the realms of animals who harm one another and devour each other, he manifests birth among them;
such acts of benefit and joy are called "Birth Stories" (Jātaka).
Though appearing to experience various desires, he constantly cultivates meditative concentration;
he confounds all evil Māras, leaving them no opportunity to gain the upper hand.
Like a flower blooming within fire, this is said to be most rare.
To practice meditative concentration while engaging in desire is rarer even than this.
Sometimes they manifest as courtesans to attract those who lust after beauty;
first drawing them in with the allure of desire, they later cause them to cultivate the wisdom of the Buddha.
Sometimes acting as governors of cities, leaders of merchants, or national preceptors;
as honored ministers and high officials, they bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
For those who are destitute, they manifest as inexhaustible treasuries.
By bestowing gifts, he eliminates poverty and leads others toward great enlightenment;
toward those who are arrogant, he manifests as a mighty athlete to crush their haughtiness and establish them in the vow for enlightenment.
To those who are terrified, they provide skillful consolation;
having removed their agitation and fear, they cause them to resolve upon the Bodhicitta.
Manifesting as seers possessing the five supernatural powers, they purely cultivate the Brahma-faring.
They cause all beings to dwell securely in morality, patience, kindness,
and compassion; or, seeing sentient beings who require immediate service,
they act as their servants or disciples to attend to them.
Through various skillful means, they cause others to delight in the True Dharma;
within all such skillful means, they are able to practice and learn well.
Such are their boundless practices and their boundless spheres of activity.
With boundless wisdom perfected, he delivers countless beings.
Even if all Buddhas were to remain for hundreds of thousands of eons praising his virtues, they could not exhaustively describe them.
"Who, having heard such a Dharma as this, would not aspire to great Bodhi?
Except for those inferior sentient beings who are entirely devoid of wisdom.

Chapter Nine: The Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality From the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Nine: The Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality. At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed all the bodhisattvas in the assembly, saying:
“How do bodhisattvas skillfully enter the gate of non-duality?
Venerable ones, you should all rely upon your own eloquence and speak according to your inclinations.
Then, among those in the assembly, various bodhisattvas spoke in succession, each according to their own inclination.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmeśvara who spoke these words:
"Arising and ceasing constitute duality.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and likewise without cessation, and thereby realize such patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this is the entry into the gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Jyotirguhya who spoke these words:
"The conceptualization of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' constitutes duality.

Because one conceives of a self, one then conceives of what belongs to self; if one realizes that there is no self, there is also nothing that belongs to self—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Animiṣa who spoke these words:
"To distinguish between grasping and non-grasping constitutes duality.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that there is no grasping, then there is nothing to be attained; because there is nothing to be attained, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither action nor cessation. To have no attachment toward any phenomena—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Śikharadhara who spoke these words:
"Defilement and purity are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas understand that defilement and purity are non-dual, they will be without discrimination. By forever severing discrimination and proceeding toward the path of cessation, this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Subhūṣaṇatārā who spoke these words:
"Distraction and conceptualization are two.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all things are without distraction and without conceptualization, then there is no mental engagement."
"To abide without distraction, without conceptualization, and without mental engagement—this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Wondrous Eye who spoke these words:
"To differentiate between the single characteristic and the absence of characteristics is duality."

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all phenomena possess neither a single characteristic, nor diverse characteristics, nor even the absence of characteristics, they then know that these single characteristics, diverse characteristics, and the absence of characteristics are equal. This is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Subāhu who spoke these words:
“The two minds of a bodhisattva and a śrāvaka constitute duality.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that the nature of these two minds is empty and like an illusion—such that there is no mind of a bodhisattva and no mind of a śrāvaka—and realize that these two minds are equal in their characteristics, being identical to illusory transformations, this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.”
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Poṣa who spoke as follows:
"The wholesome and the unwholesome are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that the nature of the wholesome and the nature of the unwholesome do not arise, and that the two phrases of 'characteristics' and 'signlessness' are equal, involving neither grasping nor abandoning—this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃha who spoke these words:
"To distinguish between what is faulty and what is faultless constitutes duality.
