If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that both the faulty and the faultless are equal, and penetrate all phenomena with vajra-like wisdom such that there is neither bondage nor liberation—this is the entry into the gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhamati who spoke as follows:
"To distinguish between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) is duality.

If bodhisattvas know that the nature of all phenomena is entirely equal, they do not give rise to dualistic conceptions regarding the outflowing and the non-outflowing; they do not cling to the conception of existence nor cling to the conception of non-existence. This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Viśuddhādhimukti who spoke thus:
"The conditioned and the unconditioned are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas understand that the nature of these two dharmas is equal, they remain far removed from all conditioned formations; their awakening-wisdom is like space, their knowledge is perfectly pure, and being without grasping or rejection, this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Nārāyaṇa who spoke these words:
"The supramundane and the mundane are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that the intrinsic nature of the mundane is empty and quiescent—neither entering nor exiting, neither flowing nor dispersing—and do not cling to it, this is the realization of the gateway to the non-dual Dharma."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Suvinītamati who spoke these words:
“Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that the nature of birth-and-death is fundamentally empty, such that there is neither transmigration nor cessation, this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.”
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Pratyakṣadarśin who spoke these words:
"Exhaustion and non-exhaustion are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas understand that there is fundamentally neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion—such that only ultimate exhaustion is called 'exhaustion,' and that which is ultimately exhausted and will never again be exhausted is called 'non-exhaustion'—then they do not fall into duality."
Furthermore, that which has an end refers to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Since within a single moment there is definitively no ending, it is therefore endless.
Because the existence of an end is absent, the endless also does not exist.
"To realize that both the finite and the infinite are empty by nature is to enter the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Samantagupta who spoke these words:
"The conceptual distinction between self and non-self constitutes duality."
If bodhisattvas understand that even a self cannot be found, how much less so a non-self?
To see that the nature of self and non-self is non-dual is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Vidyuddeva who spoke these words:
"Knowledge and ignorance are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas understand that the intrinsic nature of ignorance is itself knowledge, such that both knowledge and ignorance are unapprehendable—beyond calculation and transcending the path of calculation—and therein realize through direct insight their equality and non-duality, this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Priyadarśana who spoke these words:
"Form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness are distinguished from emptiness as two."

If one knows that the nature of the aggregates of grasping is fundamentally empty—that is, that form is empty, rather than emptiness resulting from the cessation of form—and that this applies likewise up to the aggregate of consciousness, this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāketu who spoke these words:
"The four elements and space are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that the four elements are themselves the nature of space, such that the four elements and the nature of space are entirely non-erroneous throughout the past, present, and future limits, and they thus awaken to and enter into all elements—this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Wondrous Wisdom (Sudhīmat) who spoke as follows:
"The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—these are distinguished as two."
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all things are empty by nature, they see that the self-nature of the eye is without greed, hatred, or delusion toward forms;
likewise, up to and including the self-nature of the mind, they see it as being without greed, hatred, or delusion toward mental phenomena—this is emptiness.
Having seen thus, one dwells in tranquility; this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Akṣayamati who spoke as follows:
“Generosity and the dedication [of merit] toward the nature of omniscience are each distinct and constitute two.

In this way, one discriminates between morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as between these and the dedication toward the nature of omniscience, treating each as distinct and dualistic.
If one realizes that giving itself is the nature of omniscience toward which it is dedicated, then this very nature of omniscience toward which it is dedicated is itself giving;

likewise, up to and including wisdom, the self-nature of wisdom is the nature of omniscience toward which it is dedicated, and this very nature of omniscience toward which it is dedicated is itself wisdom.
"To thoroughly understand this single principle is what constitutes the realization of the gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Profound Awakening who spoke these words:
"Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—discriminating between them constitutes duality."

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that within emptiness there are no signs whatsoever, and that within this signlessness there is also no aspiration, then within this wishlessness there is no mind, no mentation, and no consciousness that can function.
In this way, within a single gate of liberation, all three gates of liberation are fully encompassed.
To penetrate this is to enter the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Śāntendriya who spoke as follows:
“The Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are distinguished as two.

If bodhisattvas understand that the buddha-nature is itself the dharma-nature and that the dharma is itself the saṃgha-nature, then these Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and are equal to space.”
"All dharmas are likewise.
To penetrate this is to enter the gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Unobstructed Eye, who spoke these words:
"To conceptualize 'this is the view of a personal identity' and 'this is the cessation of the view of a personal identity' as two is duality.

If bodhisattvas know that the view of a personal identity is itself the cessation of the view of a personal identity, and understand it thus, they ultimately do not give rise to the view of a personal identity; regarding both the view of a personal identity and its cessation, they are without conceptualization and without discursive differentiation."
"To realize the ultimate nature of cessation of these two, without doubt, without alarm, and without fear—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Well-Subdued who spoke as follows:
"The threefold restraint of body, speech, and mind is differentiated into two."
If bodhisattvas understand that these three types of restraint are all characterized by non-action (*akṛta-lakṣaṇa*) and that their characteristics are non-dual, why is this so?
Because these three paths of action are all characterized by non-action:

the characteristic of non-action of the body is the characteristic of non-action of speech; the characteristic of non-action of speech is the characteristic of non-action of the mind; and the characteristic of non-action of the mind is the characteristic of non-action common to all phenomena. If one can accordingly enter into this characteristic of non-constructive activity, this constitutes the realization of the gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Puṇyakṣetra who spoke as follows:
"The action of transgression, the action of merit, and the immovable action are distinguished as two."
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that transgressive actions, meritorious actions, and immovable actions are all characterized by non-action, their characteristics being non-dual.

Why is this so? Because the nature and characteristics of these three types of action—transgression, merit, and immovability—are all empty. Within emptiness, there is no differentiation between the three types of action: transgression, merit, and immovability. To penetrate in this way is to enter the gateway of the non-dual dharma.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Flower Ornament (Kusumatalagarbha) who spoke these words:
"All dualistic dharmas arise from the self.

If bodhisattvas know the true nature of the self, they do not give rise to duality. Because they do not give rise to duality, there is no discernment; because there is no discernment, there is nothing to be discerned. This is the entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Vijitagarbha who spoke these words:
"The arising of all dualistic phenomena occurs through apprehension.

If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that all phenomena are ultimately unapprehendable, they will have neither grasping nor rejecting. Being free from grasping and rejecting is the entry into the gateway of non-duality."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Candrottara who spoke these words:
"Luminosity and darkness are distinguished as two.
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that in the true nature (dharmatā) there is neither darkness nor luminosity, their nature is non-dual."
Why is this so? It is like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), wherein there is neither darkness nor light;
the characteristic of all dharmas is likewise thus.
"To thus wondrously accord with the equality of all phenomena is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnamudrāhasta who spoke these words:
"To delight in nirvana and to loathe saṃsāra constitutes duality."
If bodhisattvas thoroughly understand that nirvāṇa and saṃsāra do not give rise to longing or aversion, then there is no duality between them.
Why is this? If one is bound by saṃsāra, then one seeks liberation; [but for those who understand non-duality, there is neither bondage nor seeking].
If one knows that, in the ultimate sense, there is neither birth-and-death nor bondage, why would one further seek the liberation of nirvana?
To penetrate thus—to be without bondage and without liberation, neither rejoicing in nirvana nor loathing birth-and-death—is what is called entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Maṇicūḍarāja who spoke as follows:
"The right path and the wrong path are distinguished as two.
If bodhisattvas are well able to abide securely in the right path, the wrong path will ultimately not be practiced."
Because they do not practice [such distinctions], there are no two characteristics of right and wrong paths;
because these two characteristics are removed, there is no dualistic cognition.
If there is no dualistic cognition, this constitutes the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Satyarata who spoke these words:
"The false and the real are distinguished as two.
If bodhisattvas, when contemplating the nature of reality, do not even perceive the real, how much less could they perceive the false?"
Why is this? This nature is not seen by the fleshly eye; it is seen only by the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
When one sees in this manner, there is neither seeing nor non-seeing regarding all phenomena (*dharma*); this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Thus, after the various bodhisattvas in the assembly had each spoken according to their own understanding, they simultaneously addressed Mañjuśrī, asking:
“In what way is a bodhisattva said to have entered the gateway of the non-dual dharma?”
Then Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Although all that you have said is excellent, according to my own understanding, even these explanations of yours are still termed 'duality'."

If bodhisattvas regard all phenomena as being without words, without speech, without expression, and without demonstration; as being free from all conceptual proliferation and severed from all discrimination—this is the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Then Mañjuśrī again asked the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti:
"We have each spoken according to our own inclination; now, virtuous one, you should speak: how is it that a bodhisattva is said to have 'entered the gate of the non-dual dharma'?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and said nothing. Mañjuśrī said:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"In this way, these bodhisattvas truly enter the gate of non-duality; therein, there is absolutely no conceptualization through any letters or verbal expressions.

When these bodhisattvas spoke this Dharma, five thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly all attained entry into the gate of non-duality, simultaneously realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Four;

Chapter Ten: The Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"The time for the meal is approaching, yet this Mahāsattva has not risen from his teaching of the Dharma. Where shall we, the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas, eat?"
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing his thoughts, addressed him, saying:

"Venerable sir, the Tathāgata has taught the eight liberations for the sake of the śrāvakas; you have already attained them. Do not allow your mind to be defiled by wealth or food as you listen to the True Dharma."
"If you wish to eat, wait but a moment; I shall cause you all to obtain food such as has never been experienced before.

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered such a subtle and profound meditative absorption and manifested such extraordinary supernormal powers that he showed the bodhisattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas a buddha-field in the upward direction, forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of worlds away from this buddha-land, named Sarvagandhasugandhā. Therein dwells a buddha named Gandhottamakūṭa, who currently resides there in peace, stability, and support.
In that world there is a wondrous fragrance, which is the most supreme among all the scents of humans and devas in all other Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
There are various trees there that all emit this exquisite fragrance, which universally perfumes the entire region, pervading it completely.
Within that realm, there is no mention of the two vehicles; there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas, for whom that Tathāgata preaches the Dharma.
In that world, all terraces, pavilions, palaces, walkways, groves, and garments are composed of various kinds of exquisite fragrances.

The fragrance of the food consumed by that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of bodhisattvas was most subtle and supreme, pervading immeasurable buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.

At that time, while the Tathāgata and the bodhisattvas were seated together for their meal, there was a son of heaven named Gandhavatī, who had already set out with a profound resolve for the Mahāyāna, serving and making offerings to the Tathāgata and the bodhisattvas of that land.
At that time, this entire great assembly beheld all those events in that world-system, such as the Tathāgata sitting together with the bodhisattvas to partake of food.
Then, Vimalakīrti addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Great Beings, who among you is able to go there and fetch this exquisite fragrant food?"
Due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, the assembly of bodhisattvas all remained silent.
Then, Vimalakīrti addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Why do you not now provide protection for this great assembly, such that they have become like this?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder!
You should not now disparage the assembly of bodhisattvas, as the Buddha has said:"
"Do not despise those who have not yet studied.

At that time, Vimalakīrti did not rise from his bed, but manifested before the assembly a bodhisattva—whose body was of true golden color, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and whose majestic radiance eclipsed the entire assembly—and addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!

"You should go upward; passing from this buddha-field through as many buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a buddha-world named Sarvagandhasugandhā. Therein dwells a Buddha named Gandhottamakūṭa, who is currently sitting together with various bodhisattvas to partake of a meal."
Go there and prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and you should say these words:
"In this lower region there is Vimalakīrti; he bows his head at the Buddha’s two feet and respectfully inquires of the World-Honored One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily life? Is your physical strength healthy and harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"
From afar, he circumambulated him to the right hundreds of thousands of times, prostrated at his feet, and spoke these words:

“I pray that you grant me the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal; I shall perform the Buddha-work in the Sahā world below, causing sentient beings of inferior desires and pleasures there to rejoice in great wisdom, and ensuring that the immeasurable merit and fame of the Tathāgata are heard everywhere.”

Then the emanated bodhisattva rose into the air before the assembled multitude—visible to all—and by means of swift supernatural power, reached the world of All-Wondrous Fragrance in an instant. He prostrated at the feet of the Buddha Most Supreme Fragrance Terrace and further heard these words:
"The bodhisattva from the lower direction named Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and respectfully inquires:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your physical strength healthy and harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"
From afar, he circumambulated [the Buddha] to the right hundreds of thousands of times with his mind, prostrated at his two feet, and spoke these words:

"I pray that I may receive the remnants of the World-Honored One’s meal; I shall perform the work of a Buddha in the Sahā world below, causing the sentient beings there who delight in inferior desires to rejoice in great wisdom, and also ensuring that the immeasurable merit and fame of the Tathāgata are heard everywhere."

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas from the zenith, seeing the transformed bodhisattva adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and his majestic virtue, radiance, and sublime excellence, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming:
"From where has this Great Being come?"
"Where is this Sahā world located?
And what is meant by 'inferior desires and pleasures'?
Thus he questioned the Tathāgata Most Exquisite Fragrance Terrace.
“We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this matter for us.
The Buddha told them:
“O sons of good family!

Below this buddha-field, at a distance of more than forty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of buddha-worlds away, there is a buddha-world named Sahā. Therein dwells the Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he currently resides there in peace, maintaining his presence in an age of five corruptions, proclaiming the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings of inferior disposition and desire.

In that land there is a bodhisattva named Vimalakīrti, who has already attained stable abiding in the dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation. He reveals the sublime Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas and dispatches an emanation bodhisattva to this world to extol my own body, my merits, and my name, as well as to praise the manifold virtues and adornments of this land, so as to cause the roots of goodness of those bodhisattvas to increase.
The assembly of bodhisattvas all spoke thus:
"What kind of merit does he possess to manifest such transformations, and to possess such great supernormal powers and fearlessness?
That Buddha replied:
“O sons of noble family!

These great bodhisattvas have accomplished the dharma of supreme and magnificent merit; in a single kṣaṇa, they manifest as immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas who pervade all lands throughout the ten directions, dispatching them all to perform buddha-works for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings.”

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Most Supreme Fragrance Terrace took a vessel capable of emitting all manner of exquisite fragrances, filled with food perfumed by those various wonderful scents, and placed it into the hand of the emanated bodhisattva Vimalakīrti.
At that time, nine million great bodhisattvas in that buddha-field simultaneously raised their voices and petitioned that Buddha, saying:

"We wish to go together with this manifested bodhisattva to the Sahā world in the direction below to behold Śākyamuni Tathāgata, to pay homage, serve, and attend upon him, and to hear the True Dharma; furthermore, we wish to behold, pay homage to, and serve Vimalakīrti and all the other bodhisattvas there. We pray only that the World-Honored One will grant us his protection and permission."
That Buddha said to them:
"O sons of good family!
You may go now; this is precisely the right time."
All of you should restrain your own bodily fragrances before entering the Sahā world, lest those sentient beings there become intoxicated, faint, or negligent;
all of you should likewise conceal your physical forms before entering the Sahā world, lest the bodhisattvas there feel shame or embarrassment.
"You should not conceive an inferior notion regarding that Sahā world and thereby create obstacles.
Why is this? O sons of good family!..."

All lands are like empty space; yet, because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to bring sentient beings to maturity, they manifest various kinds of buddha-fields according to the inclinations of those beings—whether defiled or pure, and lacking any fixed characteristic. Nevertheless, all buddha-fields are in reality entirely pure and without distinction.

Then the transformed bodhisattva, taking the vessel filled with food, together with nine million bodhisattvas, by the majestic power of that Buddha and the strength of Vimalakīrti, vanished from that world and, in a mere moment, suddenly appeared here in the room of Vimalakīrti in this land.
Then, Vimalakīrti miraculously manifested nine million lion thrones—subtly adorned and in no way different from the lion thrones previously occupied—upon which all the bodhisattvas were seated.
Then the emanated bodhisattva presented the vessel filled with food to Vimalakīrti.
The exquisite fragrance from that vessel pervaded the great city of Vaiśālī as well as this trichiliocosm, reaching out to its infinite and boundless limits.
Because it was perfumed with exquisite fragrances, all worlds were filled with a rich and pervasive scent.

When the brahmins, elders, householders, humans, and non-humans of the great city of Vaiśālī smelled this fragrance, they experienced something unprecedented; they marveled at it boundlessly, their bodies and minds leaping with joy.

At that time, the Licchavi king named Candracchattra, together with eighty-four thousand members of the Licchavi clan, all adorned in various ornaments, entered the house of Vimalakīrti. Seeing the great multitude of bodhisattvas within the room and the lion thrones, which were exceedingly high, broad, and magnificently decorated, he was filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He prostrated before the bodhisattvas and the great śrāvakas, then withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the earth deities and the space deities, together with the hosts of devaputras from the desire and form realms, having smelled this sublime fragrance, each came with hundreds of thousands of immeasurable retinues and entered the room of Vimalakīrti.
Then Vimalakīrti addressed the venerable Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas:
"Venerable ones, please partake of this ambrosial food bestowed by the Tathāgata."

One who eats in this manner is permeated by great compassion; do not eat this food with a limited or inferior state of mind, for if you eat it in such a way, you will certainly be unable to digest it.
At that time, among those gathered in the assembly, some inferior śrāvakas thought to themselves:
"This food is very little; how will it suffice for such a great multitude?
Then the emanated bodhisattva addressed them, saying:
"Do not measure the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit and wisdom by means of your own meager merit and wisdom. Why is this?
The waters of the four great oceans might eventually be exhausted, but this exquisite fragrant food will never come to an end."

Suppose every single sentient being in immeasurable great trichiliocosms were to consume morsels of food, each morsel equal in size to Mount Sumeru; even if they were to eat such morsels for an eon or a hundred eons, they still could not exhaust them.

Why is this so? Such food as this is produced from inexhaustible morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
Of the remains of what the Tathāgata has eaten, all sentient beings throughout immeasurable trichiliocosms could not exhaust it by eating this fragrant food for hundreds of thousands of eons.
Thereupon, the entire assembly ate this food until they were all fully satisfied, yet there was still a surplus remaining.

At that time, the śrāvakas, the bodhisattvas, and the entire gathering of humans, devas, and others, having eaten this food, found their bodies to be at ease and blissful. It was as if the bodhisattvas in the world *Sarva-sukha-vyūha* (All-Bliss-Adorned) were sustained by every form of peace and happiness; the pores of their bodies all emitted a wondrous fragrance.
It was like the various exquisite incense trees in the world *Sarva-gandha* (All-Fragrance), which constantly emit immeasurable varieties of sublime scents.
Then Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas who had come from the upper direction:
"Do you know? In that land, how does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas in that world?"
Those bodhisattvas all answered together, saying:
"The Tathāgata of our land does not preach the Dharma to bodhisattvas through words and phrases; rather, he brings all bodhisattvas to complete subdual by means of sublime fragrance."

“Those bodhisattvas each sat peacefully beneath exquisite fragrant trees. From each of those exquisite fragrant trees, various kinds of fragrances flowed forth; when those bodhisattvas smelled these exquisite fragrances, they immediately attained the samādhi called ‘Adorned with All Virtues. Having attained this samādhi, they were endowed with all the merits of a bodhisattva.”
Then those bodhisattvas who had come from the upper direction asked Vimalakīrti:
"In what manner does the Tathāgata Śākyamuni preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings in this land?"
Vimalakīrti said:

"The sentient beings of this land are all stubborn and extremely difficult to transform; therefore, the Tathāgata transforms them by means of various kinds of speech capable of subduing the stubborn."
What is meant by "various forms of speech capable of subduing the stubborn and fierce"?
It refers to proclaiming: "This is the realm of hell; this is the realm of animals; this is the realm of hungry ghosts;
this is birth in the states of no leisure; this is the impairment of the sense faculties; this is misconduct of the body..."
This is the fruit of bodily misconduct; this is verbal misconduct, and this is the fruit of verbal misconduct;
this is mental misconduct, and this is the fruit of mental misconduct; this is the taking of life, and this is the fruit of taking life;
this is taking what is not given, and this is the fruit of taking what is not given; this is sexual misconduct—
This is the fruit of sexual misconduct; this is false speech and this is the fruit of false speech;
this is divisive speech and this is the fruit of divisive speech; this is harsh speech and this is the fruit of harsh speech;
this is frivolous speech and this is the fruit of frivolous speech; this is covetousness and this is...
This is the fruit of covetousness; this is ill-will and the fruit of ill-will;
this is wrong view and the fruit of wrong view; this is stinginess and the fruit of stinginess;
this is the violation of precepts and the fruit of violating precepts; this is malice and the fruit of malice; this is laziness and the fruit of...
This is the fruit of laziness; this is mental distraction, and this is the fruit of mental distraction; this is delusion, and this is the fruit of delusion;
this is the undertaking of the training, and this is the transgression of the training;
this is the upholding of the Prātimokṣa, and this is the violation of the Prātimokṣa; this is what should be done, and this is what should not be done; this is yoga.
"This is not yoga; this is permanent abandonment, this is not permanent abandonment;
this is an obstacle, this is not an obstacle; this is an offense, this is the emergence from an offense;
this is affliction, this is purification; this is the right path, this is the wrong path; this is wholesome..."
"This is evil; this is mundane, this is supramundane;
this is blameworthy, this is blameless; this is with outflows, this is without outflows;
this is conditioned, this is unconditioned; this is a merit, this is a fault; this is suffering..."
"This is suffering; this is pleasure, this is the absence of pleasure;
this is to be weary of and detached from, this is to be rejoiced in; this is to be abandoned, this is to be cultivated;
this is saṃsāra, this is nirvāṇa"—such dharmas have immeasurable gateways.
The sentient beings of this land have minds that are stubborn and unruly; therefore, the Tathāgata teaches these various Dharma gates to settle their minds and bring them under control.
"For example, if an elephant or horse is fierce and untamable, one must apply various forms of pain and torment, even to the very marrow of its bones, before it can finally be tamed."

Thus, the sentient beings of this land are stubborn and extremely difficult to transform; the Tathāgata employs skillful means, using such earnest and piercing words of admonition to instruct them, and only thereafter do they become subdued and enter the True Dharma.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the upper direction, having heard these words, attained what they had never experienced before and all spoke thus:

“How extraordinary! The World-Honored One Śākyamuni is able to perform a difficult feat; concealing his immeasurable, noble, and precious merits, he manifests such skillful means of subduing to mature inferior and destitute sentient beings, taming and benefiting them through various gateways.”

These bodhisattvas, dwelling in this buddha-field, are likewise able to endure various forms of toil and fatigue; they have accomplished the most supreme, rare, firm, and inconceivable diligence of great compassion, supporting and propagating the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata to benefit and bring happiness to such sentient beings who are difficult to transform.
Vimalakīrti said: "So it is, Great Being!
It is exactly as you have said."

The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is able to perform what is difficult to do: concealing his immeasurable, noble, and honorable merits, he does not shrink from toil and labor as he employs skillful means to tame such stubborn and difficult-to-transform sentient beings.

These bodhisattvas and sentient beings in this buddha-field are likewise able to endure various forms of toil and fatigue; they have accomplished the most supreme, rare, firm, and inconceivable diligence of great compassion, supporting and propagating the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata to benefit and bring happiness to such immeasurable sentient beings.
“Great Being, you should know:

the merit obtained by practicing the bodhisattva path for the benefit of sentient beings in this Sahā world during a single lifetime exceeds the merit obtained by practicing the bodhisattva path for the benefit of sentient beings in all the worlds of Exquisite Fragrance for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas.”
Why is this? Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of cultivated wholesome dharmas in the Sahā world that do not exist in the pure buddha-fields of the other ten directions.
What are the ten?
First, gathering in the poor through generosity; second, gathering in those who violate the precepts through pure ethical discipline;
third, gathering in those who harbor anger through patience; fourth, gathering in those who are indolent through diligence.
Fifth, by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he gathers those with distracted minds; sixth, by means of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), he gathers those who are deluded;
seventh, by means of teaching the methods for removing the eight states of no-leisure (*akṣaṇa*), he universally gathers all sentient beings in those states of no-leisure;
eighth, by means of proclaiming the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna, he universally gathers all those who delight in inferior teachings; ninth, by means of planting...
Planting various sublime roots of goodness to universally gather in those who have not yet planted such roots;
tenth, constantly maturing all sentient beings through the four unsurpassed methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

These are the ten ways of cultivating and accumulating wholesome dharmas, which are fully present in this Sahā world-system, whereas they are not found in the pure Buddha-lands of the other ten directions.
"There are none.
Then the bodhisattvas who had come from that buddha-field spoke again:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas do the bodhisattvas of the Sahā world remain unhindered and unharmed, so that when their lives end here, they are reborn in other pure lands?"
Vimalakīrti said, “The bodhisattvas of this Sahā world who accomplish eight qualities will do so without being defiled or harmed; when their lives here end, they will be reborn in other pure lands.”
What are the eight?
First, a bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should perform virtuous deeds for sentient beings; I should not expect a virtuous reward from them."
Second, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should undergo all sufferings and afflictions on behalf of all sentient beings, and I shall dedicate all my roots of goodness entirely to them."
Third, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, with no hindrance in my heart."
Fourth, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I should subdue pride toward all sentient beings and regard them with reverence and affection as if they were Buddhas."
Fifth, the Bodhisattva’s faith and understanding are superior; having briefly heard profound sūtras that they have not previously studied or received, they harbor neither doubt nor slander.
Sixth, the Bodhisattva has no heart of jealousy toward the gains and offerings of others, and does not give rise to arrogance regarding their own gains and offerings.
Seventh, the Bodhisattva subdues their own mind, constantly reflecting upon their own faults, and does not mock the transgressions of others.
Eighth, bodhisattvas are always free from negligence regarding all wholesome dharmas and constantly delight in seeking and practicing the factors of enlightenment with diligence.
If the assembly of bodhisattvas in this Sahā world fully accomplishes these eight dharmas without impairment or injury, they will, upon the end of their lives here, be reborn in other pure lands.

While Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, and the other bodhisattvas were thus proclaiming various subtle and sublime dharmas within the great assembly, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings simultaneously resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and ten thousand bodhisattvas all realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Chapter Eleven: The Conduct of Bodhisattvas. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Conduct of Bodhisattvas. At that time, the Buddha was still in the Āmrapālī Grove, teaching the Dharma to the assembly. Suddenly, the ground where the assembly gathered became vast, expansive, and pure, and the entire multitude appeared with a golden hue.
Then Ānanda immediately addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Whose prior omen is this?”
Within this assembly, it suddenly became thus vast, magnificent, and pure, and the entire multitude appeared with a golden hue.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"This Vimalakīrti, together with Mañjuśrī, surrounded by a great multitude and respectfully attended, has resolved to come to this assembly; he has manifested these preliminary signs."
Then Vimalakīrti said to Mañjuśrī,
“We should now go together with these great beings to the presence of the Tathāgata to prostrate, serve, and gaze upon the World-Honored One, and to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.”
Mañjuśrī said, “Now is precisely the right time; we may go together.

Then Vimalakīrti manifested his supernatural power, causing the entire great assembly to remain where they were, including upon their lion-thrones, as he placed them within his right palm and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he set them down on the ground, paid homage by prostrating at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side, standing solemnly with palms joined toward the Buddha.

The great bodhisattvas descended from their lion seats, paid homage by prostrating at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side; with palms joined toward the Buddha, they stood there in solemn dignity.

The great śrāvakas, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protecting kings, also all vacated their seats, reverently prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew to stand to one side; with palms joined toward the Buddha, they stood solemnly.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having comforted the assembly of bodhisattvas and all the great multitude in accordance with the Dharma, addressed them thus:
"You great beings, each return to your respective seats as is appropriate."
At that time, the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, each returned to their original seat and sat with reverence.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“Do you see the deeds performed by the sovereign spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jyeṣṭha?”
Śāriputra replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it.
The Blessed One asked again:
"What thought do you conceive?
Śāriputra replied,
"I conceive the thought of difficulty."

I behold this Great Being’s inconceivability; his functional powers, spiritual transformations, and meritorious virtues cannot be calculated, cannot be conceived, cannot be measured, and cannot be fully extolled.
Then Ānanda immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The fragrance we have now smelled is unlike anything we have ever known before; whose fragrance is this?
The Buddha replied to him:
"This is the fragrance emitted from the pores of these bodhisattvas.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Ānanda,
"The fragrance is also being emitted from our own pores."
Ānanda asked, “By what cause does such a wondrous fragrance exist within your bodies,
O virtuous ones? Śāriputra replied:

"This was the sovereign supernatural power of the Vimalakīrti, who dispatched an emanated bodhisattva to the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Most Supreme Fragrance Terrace in the zenith. He requested the remains of the meal eaten by that Buddha and brought them to this room to offer to the great assembly; all those who partook of this food had this fragrance emerge from every one of their pores."
Then Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti,
"For how long will this sublime fragrance remain?
Vimalakīrti replied:
"Until this food has been entirely digested, its fragrance will still remain.
Ānanda asked, "How long will it take for such food as this to be completely digested?"
Vimalakīrti said:

"The power of this food will remain within the body for seven days and seven nights; after that time has passed, it may gradually be digested. Although it remains undigested for a long duration, it will cause no harm."
Venerable ones, you should know this:
if those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who have not yet entered the state of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma) eat this food, it will only be digested after they have entered that state of certainty;
if those who have not yet abandoned desire eat this food, it will only be digested after they have attained the abandonment of desire.
If those who are not yet liberated eat this food, it will only be digested once their minds have attained liberation;

if Mahāyāna bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage who have not yet resolved upon supreme enlightenment eat this food, it will only be digested once they have generated the resolve for supreme enlightenment;

and if those who have already generated the resolve for supreme enlightenment eat this food, it will only be digested once they have realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

If one who has already realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas eats this food, it will only be digested after they have necessarily established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression;

if one who has already established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression eats this food, it will only be digested after they have necessarily established themselves in the stage of being bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
"Venerable one, you should know this:

For example, in the world there is a great king of medicines named Supreme Taste (*agrasvādu*). If there are sentient beings who encounter various poisons that pervade their entire bodies, and they are given this medicine to consume, the great king of medicines will not yet be digested as long as those poisons have not all been eliminated;
only after the poisons have been extinguished does it then digest."
It is the same for those who eat this food: as long as all the poisons of the afflictions have not been entirely eliminated, so too has what is eaten not yet been digested;
only after the afflictions have been extinguished does it then become digested.
Ānanda said, "It is inconceivable;
such fragrant food provided by a Great Being as this can perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.
The Buddha then told him:
"It is so, it is so; as you have said, it is inconceivable that this fragrant food brought by Vimalakīrti can perform the work of the Buddhas for sentient beings."
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"Just as the fragrant food brought by Vimalakīrti is able to perform the work of a Buddha for sentient beings, so too,
in other world-systems throughout the ten directions, there are some buddha-fields where the work of a Buddha is performed by means of various radiances."
In some buddha-fields, the work of a Buddha is accomplished by means of the Bodhi tree;
in some buddha-fields, it is accomplished by means of various bodhisattvas; in some buddha-fields, it is accomplished by means of beholding the marks and signs of the Tathāgata’s physical body;
in some buddha-fields, it is accomplished by means of various emanated beings; or in some...
In some buddha-fields, the work of a Buddha is performed by means of various garments; in some buddha-fields, it is performed by means of various bedding and furniture;
in some buddha-fields, it is performed by means of various foods and drinks;
in some buddha-fields, it is performed by means of various groves and gardens; and in some buddha-fields, it is performed by means of various terraces and pavilions.
Furthermore, there are some buddha-fields that perform the work of a buddha by means of empty space. Why is this?
It is because sentient beings are thereby tamed through this skillful means.

"In some buddha-fields, the work of a Buddha is accomplished by proclaiming various metaphors—such as illusions, dreams, reflections, the moon in water, echoes, mirages, mirror-images, floating clouds, the city of the Gandharvas, and Indra’s net—to sentient beings through diverse words and phrases.
In other buddha-fields, the work of a Buddha is accomplished by proclaiming the various natures and characteristics of all phenomena through sounds, speech, and written characters.

In yet other buddha-fields, which are pure and tranquil, there is no speaking and no discourse, no censure and no praise, no seeking after anything and no conceptual proliferation, no expression and no demonstration; therein, the sentient beings to be converted naturally realize and enter into the natures and characteristics of all phenomena due to this very silence, thereby accomplishing the work of a Buddha."
"In this way, you should know:
the Buddha-lands of the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions are infinite in number, and the Buddha-activities they perform are likewise immeasurable.

To state it briefly, all the Buddhas' deportment, movements, enjoyments, and actions serve to discipline and subdue the sentient beings who are to be transformed; therefore, all of these are termed 'Buddha-activities.'"

"Furthermore, regarding all the four māras and the eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction that exist in the world, by which sentient beings are tormented, all Tathāgatas perform the Buddha-work for all living beings precisely through these very phenomena."
"You should now know this:
this Dharma-gate is called 'Awakening into All Buddha-Dharmas.

If Bodhisattvas enter this Dharma-gate, although they see all Buddha-lands adorned with the purity of immeasurable and vast merits, they do not give rise to joy or greed; and although they see all Buddha-lands devoid of merit and filled with impurity, they do not give rise to sorrow or anger. Instead, toward all Buddhas, they generate the highest degree of faith, delight, and reverence, exclaiming, 'How unprecedented! "

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are equal and perfect in all merits—because they have attained the ultimate, true equality of all phenomena—and yet, desiring to bring sentient beings of diverse dispositions to maturity, they manifest various distinct Buddha-lands.
"You should now know this:
just as the various Buddha-fields differ in the excellence or inferiority of their underlying lands, yet there is no distinction whatsoever in the space above them,
so too should you understand this:"

Although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest various and diverse physical bodies in order to bring sentient beings to maturity without obstruction, their ultimate perfection of merit and wisdom is entirely without distinction.

"You should now know this: all Tathāgatas are entirely equal—namely, in their most supreme, perfect, and infinite physical form and majestic radiance; in their primary marks and secondary signs; in their noble lineage and status; in their pure ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; in their powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-qualities; in their great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness; in their dignified deportment, conduct, right practice, and lifespan; in their teaching of the Dharma, delivering and maturing sentient beings; and in their pure Buddha-fields—all of these are entirely equal."

Because all the Buddha-dharmas of all Tathāgatas are entirely equal, supremely perfect, ultimate, and inexhaustible, they are therefore all equally named "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha), named "Tathāgata," and named "Buddha."
"You should know this now:

even if I were to analyze and explain these three phrases in detail, and you were to remain for an eon listening and receiving them without interruption, you would not be able to exhaust them even by the end of your lifespan."

Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were like Ānanda—possessing the dhāraṇī of mindfulness and being foremost in erudition—and were to dwell for an entire kalpa listening and receiving [the teachings] without interruption, they could not exhaust them even by the end of their lifespans.
Regarding these three sublime meanings—the Perfectly Awakened One, the Tathāgata, and the Buddha—none are able to fully proclaim or definitively resolve them, except for the Buddhas themselves.
Thus one should know:
the merits of the Buddhas' bodhi are immeasurable, and their unimpeded, wondrous eloquence is inconceivable.
When these words had been spoken, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall not dare to claim that I am foremost among those who possess mindfulness, dhāraṇī, and great learning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"You should not now give rise to thoughts of despondency. Why is this?
"Since long ago, I have only said that among the assembly of śrāvakas, you are foremost in mindfulness, dhāraṇī, and extensive learning, but not among the bodhisattvas.
You should now desist; those who possess wisdom ought not to measure the affairs of the bodhisattvas."
You should now know this:
while the depth and shallowness of all great oceans may still be measured, no one can fathom the great ocean of a bodhisattva’s wisdom, mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇī, and eloquence.
"You disciples, set aside the sphere of activity of the bodhisattvas, which you should not attempt to conceive;

even in the time it takes to eat a single meal, the miraculous displays and transformations manifested by Vimalakīrti through his supernormal powers cannot be matched by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even if they were to employ their own powers of transformation for hundreds of thousands of great kalpas."
Then all the bodhisattvas who had come from the direction above rose, prostrated themselves before Śākyamuni, joined their palms in reverence, and said:
“World-Honored One!
When we first arrived and saw this buddha-field with its various impurities, we conceived inferior thoughts; now we all repent, feel ashamed, and renounce such a mind.”

Why is this? The skillful means within the realm of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, they manifest buddha-fields in whatever manner accords with the diverse inclinations of those beings.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will grant us a brief teaching, so that we may return to the world of All Sublime Fragrances and, by means of this Dharma, constantly keep the Tathāgata in mind.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One addressed those bodhisattvas who had come to him, saying:
“Good son! There is a liberation dharma-gate for bodhisattvas called ‘The Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible. You should now respectfully receive it and diligently practice and study it.
What is meant by ‘the exhaustible and the inexhaustible’?”
That which is said to be finite is the conditioned, characterized by the dharmas of arising and ceasing;
that which is said to be infinite is the unconditioned, devoid of the dharmas of arising and ceasing.
“A Bodhisattva should neither exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor should they abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
How does a Bodhisattva not exhaust the conditioned?

It means that Bodhisattvas do not abandon great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and do not relinquish great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); they never forget the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) and the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) that they have previously generated, holding them dear and precious; they never grow weary in maturing sentient beings; they never forsake the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); they protect and uphold the true Dharma without sparing even their own body or life; and they seek to practice all virtues without ever reaching satiety.”

They constantly delight in skillfully establishing the dedication of merit; they seek the true Dharma without ever becoming weary; and they expound the teachings of the Dharma without growing tired of acting as teachers.

They always rejoice in gazing upon and serving the Buddhas; therefore, though they undergo birth and death, they have no fear, and though they encounter prosperity or decline, they feel neither elation nor dejection.
Toward those who have not yet studied, they never treat them with contempt or arrogance; and toward those who have already studied...

He regards [the teacher] with reverence as a Buddha; he is able to reflect correctly upon the defilements amidst their mixture, and is able to remain free from attachment to the pleasures of seclusion.
He has never tasted a craving for his own happiness, and with a deep heart, he rejoices in the happiness of others.

Regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti) that he practices, he perceives them as if they were hell and does not relish them.
They conceive of the realms, destinies, and the cycle of birth and death they traverse as a royal park, never feeling weary or seeking to escape from them;
they regard those who beg from them as virtuous friends, relinquishing all they possess without any sense of regret or stinginess;
they give rise to the thought of dedication toward omniscience; they conceive of those who violate the precepts as beings to be rescued and protected; and regarding the perfections...

One should regard one’s parents as those whose wishes one must swiftly fulfill; one should regard the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as wings that carry one along, never letting them reach a final end;
one should constantly and diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas; one should always delight in adorning all buddha-fields;
one should, with a profound mind, rejoice in and praise the buddha-fields of others; and one should be able to swiftly accomplish the adornment of one’s own buddha-field.
"To adorn oneself with the perfection of the primary and secondary marks, one practices pure and unimpeded great giving;
to purify the adornment of body, speech, and mind, one remains far removed from all transgressions and unwholesome dharmas;
to make body and mind firm and resilient, one remains far removed from all anger, resentment, and afflictions."
To ensure that what is cultivated reaches swift completion, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death through countless eons;
to cause one's own mind to dwell with courageous firmness, one listens to the Buddha’s immeasurable merits without weariness;
and wishing to forever destroy the enemy of afflictions, one skillfully cultivates the sword and staff of prajñā.
Desiring to bear the heavy burden of all sentient beings, they seek thorough and complete knowledge of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases;
desiring to subdue all hosts of Māra, they exert fervent diligence without ever succumbing to indolence;
and desiring to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma, they remain free from pride while diligently seeking the skillful wisdom of transformation.
They are cherished and respected by all the world as they receive and transform beings; they always delight in practicing and cultivating [the path], possessing few desires and being content.
They are forever untainted by worldly dharmas, yet are able to accord with all the world;
their deportment is never impaired, yet they are able to manifest all manner of activities.
"May they give rise to various supernormal powers and sublime wisdom to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings;
may they receive and uphold all the True Dharma they have heard to give rise to sublime knowledge, right mindfulness, and dhāraṇī;
and may they give rise to the sublime wisdom that discerns the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings in order to sever all their doubts."
They realize various forms of unimpeded eloquence, expounding the True Dharma without ever encountering obstruction;
they diligently cultivate the ten paths of pure wholesome action to receive the sublime joy and happiness of humans and devas;
and they vigorously advance in the practice of the four immeasurable wisdoms to correctly open the path to the Brahma heavens.
To attain the supreme and wondrous voices of all Buddhas, they entreat them to teach the Dharma and joyfully praise their excellence;
to attain the supreme and wondrous deportment of all Buddhas, they constantly cultivate the extraordinary tranquility of the three karmas;
and to cause their cultivation to increase and excel moment by moment, they maintain a mind free from defilement or obstruction regarding all phenomena.
To be a well-disciplined leader of the assembly of bodhisattvas, they constantly exhort sentient beings to study the Mahāyāna;
to ensure that all their merits are not lost or destroyed, they are at all times ever-vigilant and free from negligence;
and to cause all roots of goodness to progress ever further, they always delight in cultivating and refining various great vows.
In order to adorn all buddha-fields, one should constantly and diligently cultivate vast roots of goodness;
in order that what has been cultivated may ultimately be inexhaustible, one should constantly practice the skillful means of dedication.
“O sons of good family!
To practice this Dharma is called a bodhisattva’s non-exhaustion of the conditioned.
How does a bodhisattva not dwell in the unconditioned?
That is to say, although bodhisattvas practice emptiness, they do not delight in realizing it;
although they practice signlessness, they do not delight in realizing it;
although they practice wishlessness, they do not delight in realizing it.
Although they practice non-action, they do not delight in realizing that state of non-action;
although they contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, their minds never grow weary of or satisfied with roots of goodness;
and although they contemplate that everything in the world is suffering, they intentionally take birth within saṃsāra.
Although they delight in observing that there is no self within, they do not ultimately abandon their own bodies;
although they delight in observing that there are no sentient beings without, they constantly transform and guide others with minds free from weariness;
although they observe that nirvāṇa is ultimately quiescent, they do not ultimately fall into extinction.
Although they contemplate detachment as ultimate peace and happiness, they do not ultimately weary of or seek to abandon body and mind;
although they delight in observing the absence of the ālayavijñāna, they do not discard the treasury of pure and white dharmas;
although they observe that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, they constantly shoulder the task of benefiting sentient beings.
Although they contemplate the untainted, they do not cease from the cycle of birth and death;
although they contemplate non-action, they carry out deeds to bring all sentient beings to maturity;
although they contemplate selflessness, they do not abandon great compassion for sentient beings.
Although they contemplate non-arising, they do not fall into the fixed positions of the two vehicles;
although they contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, they do not make the merit they cultivate empty and quiescent;
although they contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately detached, they do not detach from the wisdom they cultivate.
Although they contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately without reality, they always abide in perfect contemplation;
although they contemplate that all phenomena are ultimately without a master, they always exert themselves with diligence to seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*);
and although they contemplate that all phenomena are forever without marks, they establish the lineage of the Buddha within the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
“O sons of good family!
To practice this Dharma is called ‘the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned.
Furthermore, sons of good family!”

Because Bodhisattvas constantly and diligently cultivate and accumulate the provisions of merit, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they constantly and diligently cultivate and accumulate the provisions of wisdom, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they have accomplished great loving-kindness without deficiency, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they have accomplished great compassion without deficiency, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they bring to ultimate fulfillment all Buddha-dharmas, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they fulfill the Buddha’s form-body adorned with all the marks and signs, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they realize the Buddha’s wisdom-body consisting of all the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they skillfully employ expedient means to transform sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they skillfully observe with subtle and wondrous wisdom, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they cultivate and purify the Buddha-lands until they are ultimately fulfilled, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because the Buddha-body dwells in peace, eternally inexhaustible, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they constantly perform deeds that benefit sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because they receive and uphold the meaning of the Dharma without ceasing, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Because they accumulate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that are eternally inexhaustible, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because the power of their roots of goodness sustains them without interruption or destruction, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they desire to fulfill their original vows, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they do not long for eternal quiescent extinction (*atyanta-nirvāṇa*), they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because their resolute intention (*āśaya*) is perfectly pure, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because their superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) is perfectly pure, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Because they constantly sport with the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they do not abide in the unconditioned; because their Buddha-knowledge and six supernormal powers are perfectly fulfilled, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because the provisions for the perfections (*pāramitā*) are complete, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because that which was originally contemplated is not yet fully realized, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they never tire of gathering the treasures of the Dharma, they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because they do not delight in seeking only a small portion of the Dharma, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because their firm vows never regress, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they are able to bring those vows to ultimate fulfillment, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they accumulate all the medicines of the sublime Dharma, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they bestow the medicine of the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each, they do not exhaust the conditioned.

Because they fully comprehend the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings, they do not abide in the unconditioned; because they pacify and eliminate the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings, they do not exhaust the conditioned.
"O sons of good family!

In this way, the bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned nor abide in the unconditioned; this is called dwelling securely in the liberation dharma-gate of the exhausted and the inexhaustible, which you all should diligently practice and study.

At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Most Excellent Fragrance-Pavilion in the world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā, having heard this exposition of the liberation door of "the exhaustible and the inexhaustible," their minds were inspired and encouraged by the unfolding of the Dharma. They all rejoiced greatly, their bodies and minds leaping with joy, and they made offerings to the World-Honored One, to the bodhisattvas, and to this taught Dharma-door of the exhaustible and the inexhaustible, using immeasurable varieties of exquisite fragrant flowers and various ornaments.
Furthermore, they scattered various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers throughout the trichiliocosm, such that the ground was covered with them to a depth that submerged their knees.

At that time, the bodhisattvas paid homage by prostrating at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and extolled the praises of Śākyamuni, the other bodhisattvas, and the Dharma taught. Suddenly, they vanished from this buddha-field and, after a mere moment, arrived in that land.
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Five;
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
12. Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata:
Chapter Twelve At that time, the World-Honored One asked Vimalakīrti:
"Good man!..."
"You previously came here wishing to behold the body of the Tathāgata; how, then, should you behold the Tathāgata?
Vimalakīrti replied, "I behold the Tathāgata as seeing nothing at all; it is in this manner that I behold him."
Why is this? As I contemplate the Tathāgata, he does not come from the past, nor does he go toward the future, nor does he abide in the present. Why is that?

I contemplate the Tathāgata’s form as having the nature of *tathatā*, yet its nature is not form; its sensation has the nature of *tathatā*, yet its nature is not sensation; its perception has the nature of *tathatā*, yet its nature is not perception; its formations have the nature of *tathatā*, yet their nature is not formations; and its consciousness has the nature of *tathatā*, yet its nature is not consciousness.
Not abiding in the four elements, it is identical to the realm of empty space;
not arising from the six sense bases, it transcends the paths of the six faculties;
unmixed with the three realms, it remains far removed from the three defilements.
In accordance with the three liberations, one follows until the attainment of the three insights (*trividyā*).
It is not insight yet it is insight; it is not attainment yet it is attainment, reaching the limit of all phenomena where there is no obstruction.
The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is not a limit; suchness (*tathatā*) is not suchness. Within the realm of suchness, one never dwells; with the wisdom of suchness, one is forever non-associated.
The nature of the object and wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from both; it is not produced by causes, nor does it arise from conditions;
it is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither its own mark nor another’s mark; it is neither a single mark nor diverse marks;
it is neither identical to the characterized nor separate from the characterized; it is neither the same as the characterized nor different.
The characterized is neither identical to the characterizer nor separate from the characterizer;
it is neither the same as the characterizer nor different from the characterizer; it is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle stream;
it is not here, not there, and not in between; it is not internal, not external, not both, and not neither.
It has not gone, it will not go, and it does not go now; it has not come, it will not come, and it does not come now.
It is neither cognition nor object, neither the cognizer nor the cognized, neither hidden nor manifest, neither dark nor light;
it is without abiding and without going, without name and without mark.
It is neither strong nor weak; it does not abide in spatial dimensions, nor is it separate from spatial dimensions.
It is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned. It is neither eternally extinguished nor non-extinguished.
There is nothing whatsoever that can be demonstrated, and no meaning whatsoever that can be explained. There is neither giving nor stinginess.
There is no precept and no transgression; no patience and no anger; no diligence and no indolence;
no concentration and no distraction; no wisdom and no folly; no truth and no falsehood;
no exiting and no entering; no going and no coming; all speech and activity are utterly extinguished.

It is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit; neither worthy of offerings nor unworthy of offerings; neither the grasper nor the grasped; neither the subject of apprehension nor the object of apprehension; neither characterized nor uncharacterized; neither acting nor non-acting; it is incalculable and free from all calculation; unimpeded and free from all impediments; without increase and without decrease.
Equal and equal, identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and coextensive with the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

It is neither the subject that designates nor the object designated; it transcends all natures of designation. It is neither the means of measurement nor the object measured; it transcends all natures of measurement. It has no orientation and no aversion; it transcends all orientations and aversions. It has no valor and no timidity; it transcends all valor and timidity. It is neither great nor small, neither broad nor narrow. It is without seeing and without hearing, without perception and without cognition.

Free from all fetters, he is serenely liberated; he realizes the equality of the knowledge of all-knowledge, attains non-duality with all sentient beings, and reaches the undifferentiated nature of all phenomena. Pervading all things, he is without fault or transgression, without turbidity or impurity, and without obstruction or attachment. He is free from all conceptualization, without action or arising, without falsehood or reality, without origination or cessation, without past or future, without fear or defilement, without sorrow or joy, and without weariness or delight. He cannot be taken as an object by any conceptual discrimination and cannot be described by any names or expressions.
“World-Honored One!
The physical marks of the Tathāgata are such as these; one should contemplate them in this way and not otherwise.
To contemplate in this manner is called right contemplation; to contemplate otherwise is called wrong contemplation.”
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
from where did this Vimalakīrti pass away to come and be born here in this Sahā world?"
The Blessed One said,
"You should question him.
Thereupon, Śāriputra questioned Vimalakīrti.
“From where did you pass away to be reborn in this land?
Vimalakīrti replied, “Indeed, Śāriputra!”
“Since you have universally known and realized all phenomena, is there even the slightest phenomenon that can undergo death or birth?
Śāriputra replied, “Indeed, Vimalakīrti!”
"There is not even the slightest dharma that can undergo death or birth.
Vimalakīrti said:
"If all dharmas are fully known and realized such that there is neither death nor birth, why do you ask: [why does one die and why is one born?]"
"From where did you pass away to come and be born in this land?
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what do you think?
"From where did these men and women created by illusion pass away to come and be born here?
Śāriputra replied,
"It is impossible to establish the passing away or birth of men and women created by illusion."
Vimalakīrti said,
"Has the Tathāgata not taught that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations?
Śāriputra replied:
"So it is, so it is," Vimalakīrti said.
"If all phenomena are by their very nature and characteristics like illusions and transformations, why does your reverence suddenly ask this?"
“From where did you pass away to come and be born in this land?
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
“passing away” is the characteristic of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and “being born” is the characteristic of the continuity of all conditioned phenomena.
"Although a bodhisattva passes away, they do not sever the characteristics of the practice of all wholesome dharmas;
although a bodhisattva is born, they do not continue the characteristics of the practice of any unwholesome dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“There is a buddha-world named Abhirati; the Tathāgata therein is named Akṣobhya. This Vimalakīrti, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, has passed away from that land and come to be born in this world.”
Śāriputra said:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
Such a Great Being is truly unprecedented, for he is able to leave that pure Buddha-field and come to delight in this place so full of manifold impurities."
Vimalakīrti said: "Indeed, Śāriputra!
What do you think?"
"How could the light of the sun dwell together with the darkness of the world?
Śāriputra replied, "No, householder!"
"As soon as the sun rises, all darkness is extinguished.
Vimalakīrti asked,
"For what reason does the sun travel over Jambudvīpa?"
Śāriputra said,
"It is for the purpose of removing darkness and providing illumination.
Vimalakīrti replied:

"In this way, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, takes birth in defiled Buddha-fields; yet he does not dwell in association with any afflictions, but merely extinguishes the darkness of the afflictions of all living beings."

At that time, the great assembly all conceived a deep longing, desiring to behold the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, as well as the pure buddha-field of Abhirati adorned with sublime merits.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, addressed Vimalakīrti: "Good son!

Now all the great assembly here, including the various seers and gods, have conceived a deep longing and desire to see the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and his host of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the pure buddha-field of Abhirati, adorned with sublime merits. You should manifest it for them so that their aspiration may be fulfilled."
At that time, Vimalakīrti thought to himself:
"Without rising from this seat, I shall use my supernormal powers to swiftly transport the world of Abhirati,
along with its Cakravāḍa mountains, groves, gardens, ponds, springs, streams, valleys, and great..."
The oceans and rivers; the peaks and valleys surrounded by all the Sumeru mountains; the sun, moon, and constellations;
the palaces of the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, and Brahmā;
the assemblies together with the bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas; and the villages, cities, towns, hamlets, provinces, and royal capitals.
Furthermore, within their respective households, among men and women, great and small, and so forth—as extensively described—the great Bodhi tree of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Acala;
the assembly of the ocean-like multitude sitting peacefully to hear the Dharma;
and the various precious lotuses that travel to the worlds of the ten directions to perform Buddha-works for the sake of sentient beings—all these appeared spontaneously as three jeweled stairways.

It surged upward from Jambudvīpa to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven atop Mount Sumeru. Desiring to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya and to hear the Dharma, beings from this world ascended these jeweled stairways at all times;
likewise, the people of Jambudvīpa also ascended these jeweled stairways whenever they wished to view the groves and palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

In this manner, he took up the entire pure world-system of Abhirati—composed of immeasurable merits, extending from the water-circle below to the Akaniṣṭha heaven above—and placed it all within his right palm, as easily as a potter’s wheel or a string of flowers, and brought it into this world to show it to the great assembly.

Having formed this thought, Vimalakīrti did not rise from his bed, but entered into samādhi and manifested such a sublime supernatural power that he swiftly severed and took the world of Abhirati, placed it upon his right palm, and brought it into this realm.
The śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of that land, as well as the great assembly of humans and devas who possessed the divine eye, were all struck with terror and cried out in unison:
"Who is taking us away?"
"Who will take us away?
We pray only that the World-Honored One may protect and deliver us; we pray only that the Sugata may protect and deliver us.
Then, the Buddha Akṣobhya, employing skillful means to transform sentient beings, addressed them, saying:
“Sons of good family!
Do not be afraid, do not be afraid.
This is brought forth by the supernatural power of Vimalakīrti; it is not within my capability.”

The assembly of gods, humans, and others in that land who were beginners and had not yet attained the superior supernormal power of the divine eye all remained peaceful, neither knowing nor seeing [anything].
Upon hearing these words, they all asked one another in alarm: "Where should we go now?"
"Although the land of Abhirati has entered this realm, its various characteristics neither decrease nor increase, and the world of Endurance (Sahā) is not crowded.
Even though these two realms are thus intermingled, each group perceives its own dwelling as no different from before."
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni addressed the great assembly:
"Do you all, O seers and immortals, behold the adorned buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the world-system Abhirati, as well as the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and others?"
All of them replied:
"World-Honored One!
We have seen it."
