Then, Vimalakīrti, by means of his supernatural power, manifested various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers and other powdered incenses for the great assembly, causing them to scatter these as offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Akṣobhya Tathāgata, and all the bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly:

"You who are seers and divine beings, and who wish to accomplish such adornment of a Buddha-land as a bodhisattva, should all follow and learn the various bodhisattva practices originally cultivated by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."

When Vimalakīrti manifested the realm of Abhirati through his supernormal powers, eighty-four nayutas of beings—both humans and devas—from this Sahā world simultaneously resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, all vowing to be reborn in the world of Abhirati.
The World-Honored One bestowed this prediction upon them all:
"You shall all be reborn in the buddha-field where the Tathāgata Akṣobhya dwells.

Then, through his supernormal powers, Vimalakīrti transported this world of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the assembly of bodhisattvas, desiring to benefit the sentient beings of this realm. Having completed that task, he returned them to their original place; both groups saw them separated from one another.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Have you already beheld the world-system of Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and the bodhisattvas?"
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One,
I have seen it.”

May all sentient beings dwell in such adorned buddha-fields; may all sentient beings achieve such perfect merits of merit and wisdom, becoming in every way like the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; and may all sentient beings obtain sovereign supernormal powers like those of Vimalakīrti.
“World-Honored One!

We have truly attained a great victory in being able to behold and draw near to such a Great Being. One should know that any sentient beings who merely hear this sublime Dharma-gate have already attained a great victory; how much more so those who, having heard it, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, master it thoroughly, and extensively explain it to others?”
How much more so for those who practice with skillful means and diligence!
"If sentient beings obtain such a supreme dharma-gate as this in their hands, they have thereby acquired a treasury of the jewels of the Dharma;
if sentient beings believe in and understand such a supreme dharma-gate as this, they have thereby succeeded to the lineage of all Buddhas."
In this continuous succession, if sentient beings read and recite such a sublime Dharma-gate, they shall become Bodhisattvas and companions to the Buddhas;
if sentient beings receive and uphold such a sublime Dharma-gate, they shall thereby embrace the unsurpassed True Dharma;
and if one makes offerings to those who study this Dharma, one should know that the Buddha is present within their very home.
Come! If one copies and makes offerings to such a sublime Dharma-gate, one thereby embraces all merit and the knowledge of all modes;
if one rejoices in such a Dharma-gate, one thereby establishes a great Dharma-sacrifice;
and if one expounds even a single four-line verse of such a sublime Dharma-gate for others...
It is said that such a person has already attained the stage of non-retrogression; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family can believe,
understand, accept, cherish, and contemplate such an excellent Dharma-gate, they have already received the prophecy of unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Chapter 13: Dharma-Offering. Thus have I heard. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! [The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, Chapter Thirteen: Dharma-Offering. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

Although I have heard from the Buddha and Mañjuśrī hundreds of thousands of various distinctions among Dharma-gates, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate of liberation as this inconceivable, sovereign, and miraculous transformation that has been explained.

As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, if any sentient beings hear such a Dharma-gate as this and believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and extensively explain it to others, they are certainly vessels of the Dharma beyond any doubt; how much more so those who apply themselves with diligence to practice it according to the principle?

In this way, these sentient beings close off all perilous paths to the evil realms and open up all level roads to the auspicious realms; they constantly behold all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, subdue all heterodoxies and rival doctrines, and annihilate all violent and malevolent demonic armies; they purify the path to Bodhi, establish themselves in wondrous enlightenment, and tread upon the path traversed by the Tathāgatas.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate as it has been taught, and who believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, and even practice it diligently and according to the principle, I shall, together with all my retinue, reverently make offerings to these sons and daughters of good family.”
“World-Honored One!

Should there be any villages, towns, settlements, cities, or royal capitals where this Dharma-gate is upheld, recited, explained, and circulated, I, together with all my retinue, shall go to those places for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Those who have not yet developed faith, I shall cause to believe; those who already have faith, I shall protect in accordance with the Dharma, ensuring they remain free from obstacles and difficulties.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said; you are now able to rejoice in this subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate spoken by the Tathāgata."
O Lord of Devas,
you should know that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present is briefly revealed within this very Dharma-gate.

Therefore, if any sons or daughters of good family hear this Dharma-gate as it has been taught, and believe in it, understand it, accept and uphold it, read and recite it, master it, explain it extensively for others, transcribe it, and make offerings to it, they are thereby making offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
"Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of Devas!

Suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas—like a thicket of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, hemp, rice, or mountain forests—and if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to, for an eon or more than an eon, honor, respect, praise, and serve them, offering to those Tathāgatas all the most excellent articles of comfort and pleasure belonging to gods and humans, and all the most excellent dwellings of comfort and pleasure.

After their parinirvāṇa, one makes offerings to each of their entire-body relics by constructing stūpas out of the seven precious jewels—equal in length and breadth to the world-system of the four continents, towering in height as far as the Brahma Heaven, and adorned with the most exquisite of all things: pillars, wheels, discs, incense, flowers, banners, canopies, various treasures, and music. Having thus established for each Tathāgata a stūpa adorned with the seven jewels, one continues for an eon or more than an eon to reverently honor, respect, praise, and make offerings to them with every kind of supreme and wonderful celestial and human flower garlands, burning incense, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, canopies, jeweled standards, lamps, various treasures, music, and all manner of ritual implements.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family obtain much merit by reason of this?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
Inconceivable, Sugata!
Even in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, one could not describe the measure of that mass of merit.”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "So it is, so it is.
I shall now further address you with words of truth:

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this inconceivable, sovereign, and miraculous dharma-gate of liberation, and believes, understands, upholds, recites, and explains it, the mass of merit they obtain will be far greater than that.
Why is this? Because the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas arises from this; only the offering of the Dharma can truly honor such a Dharma-gate, not the offering of material wealth.
"Lord of Devas, you should know that because the merit of unsurpassed bodhi is vast, the merit of making offerings to this Dharma is exceedingly great.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"In the distant past, inconceivable, immeasurable, and incalculable great kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Bhaisajyarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One."
That Buddha-world is named Great Adornment (Mahāvyūha), and its eon is named Pure Adornment (Vyūhaśuddhi).

The lifespan of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja abiding in the world is twenty intermediate eons; his assembly of śrāvakas numbers thirty-six koṭi-nayuta, and his assembly of bodhisattvas numbers twelve koṭi.

At that time, there was a Wheel-Turning King named Ratnacchattra, who possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four great continents; he was endowed with a thousand sons who were handsome, courageous, and capable of subduing enemy armies.

At that time, King Ratnacchattra, together with his retinue, for five full intermediate kalpas, reverently honored, respected, praised, and served the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, offering him all manner of supreme and exquisite articles of comfort and pleasure belonging to devas and humans, as well as all supreme and exquisite dwellings of peace and happiness.
After five kalpas had passed, King Ratnacchattra addressed his thousand sons:
"You should know this:
I have already made offerings to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; you now should likewise offer worship and support as I have done."
Thereupon, the thousand sons, having heard the instruction of their father the King, received it with joy and reverence, and all said:
"Excellent! We shall all act in unison for the full five intermediate kalpas."

Together with his retinue, he reverently honored, respected, praised, and served the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, offering as gifts and worship all manner of supreme and exquisite articles of comfort and bliss for humans and devas, as well as all supreme and exquisite dwellings of peace and happiness.
At that time, there was a prince named Candracchattra who, dwelling alone in seclusion, reflected thus:

"We are now offering such earnest, respectful, and reverent worship to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja; is there perhaps any other form of reverent worship that is more supreme, more excellent, or superior to this?"
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, a deity in the sky above uttered a voice, addressing the prince:
"Prince Candracchattra,
you should know that among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is the most supreme."
He then asked:
"What is called the 'Dharma-offering'?
The deva replied:
"Candracchattra!
You should go and ask the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja:
'World-Honored One!'"
"What is called the 'Dharma-offering'?
The Buddha shall explain and reveal it to you in detail.

Having heard these words from the deva, Prince Candracchattra immediately went to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja. With respectful and earnest devotion, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then stood to one side, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is the most supreme. What are the characteristics of this offering of the Dharma?”
The Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the prince, saying: "Candracchattra,

you should know that 'Dharma-offering' refers to the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas— subtle and profound, appearing as if they were even more profound, extremely difficult for all the world to believe and accept, difficult to traverse, difficult to see, mysterious and subtle, stainless and definitive in meaning, and not known through conceptual discrimination."

This King of Sūtras, a dhāraṇī subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, is sealed with the seal of the Buddha; it analytically reveals the irreversible wheel of Dharma, from which the six pāramitās arise, and it skillfully encompasses all that should be embraced.

It follows correctly the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) and directly brings forth the seven limbs of awakening (saptabodhyaṅga). It eloquently expounds and reveals great loving-kindness and great compassion, rescuing and establishing all classes of sentient beings, and causing them to remain far removed from all views, tendencies, and demonic adversaries.

It analytically elucidates the profound dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), explaining the absence of a self within, the absence of sentient beings without, and the ultimate non-existence of a life-principle or a nourisher in between these two.
The nature of the *pudgala* is empty; it is signless, wishless, unconditioned, and unarisen;
it is associated with that which can lead to sublime awakening and can turn the wheel of Dharma; it is universally respected, praised, and honored by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others;
it guides sentient beings through the great Dharma-offering, fulfills the great Dharma-sacrifice for sentient beings, and is embraced by all noble ones.
It develops all the sublime practices of bodhisattvas; it is the refuge for the true meaning of the Dharma, from which the most supreme unimpededness arises.

It explains in detail that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and quiescent, giving rise to the four summaries of the Dharma (*dharmoddāna*). It eliminates all stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, malice, laziness, distracted mindfulness, and faulty wisdom; it strikes terror into all the heterodox arguments, evil views, and attachments of external paths; it develops the superior power of all virtuous qualities in sentient beings; and it crushes and subdues all the hosts of Māra’s evil armies.

Praised by all Buddhas and noble sages, capable of eliminating all the great sufferings of birth and death and capable of revealing all the great bliss of nirvāṇa, this sutra is taught by the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions. If one joyfully listens to, believes and understands, receives and maintains, reads and recites, masters, contemplates, and examines its profound meaning; if one makes it manifest, establishes it, analyzes and reveals it so that it appears clearly before one, and further extensively proclaims and explains it for others, employing skillful means to protect and uphold the True Dharma—all such acts are called "Dharma-offering."
"Furthermore, Candracchattra!
As for the 'Dharma-offering,' it refers to the subduing of all phenomena according to the Dharma, as well as the practice of all phenomena according to the Dharma."

In accordance with dependent origination, they abandon all false views and cultivate the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They realize and enter into selflessness and the absence of sentient beings.
Regarding all causes and conditions, they harbor no opposition, no contention, and raise no dissent; they are free from "I" and "mine," and remain without grasping.

One relies on the meaning and not on the letter; one relies on wisdom and not on consciousness; one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning and never relies on sūtras of provisional meaning that speak of worldly conventions, thereby giving rise to attachment; one relies on the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and never relies on the view of a person (pudgala) that perceives anything as attainable.

Realizing all phenomena according to their intrinsic nature and characteristics, they enter the state beyond storage and inclusion, extinguishing the *ālayavijñāna*. They bring to rest ignorance through to old age and death; they bring to rest sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and feverish affliction. Observing these twelve links of dependent origination as an inexhaustible and ever-arising process, they vow that all sentient beings shall abandon all dogmatic views.
"This is what is called the supreme offering of Dharma.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:

"When Prince Candracchattra heard from the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja this teaching on the supreme offering of Dharma, he attained the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti). He immediately removed his precious robes and various ornaments and offered them as a gift to the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:"
“World-Honored One!
I vow that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I shall receive and uphold the True Dharma, performing Dharma-offerings and protecting the True Dharma.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will employ his supernormal powers to bestow his majestic authority upon me, so that I may be free from obstacles, subdue Māra and his enemies, and protect the True Dharma while cultivating the bodhisattva practices.”
When the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja knew that Candracchattra’s superior intention was thus, he bestowed upon him this prophecy:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you shall be able to protect the city of the Dharma."

At that time, having heard the prophecy, the prince was filled with joy and exultation; he then, within the holy Dharma-teachings of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja while he remained in the world, renounced the life of a householder out of pure faith and went forth into the homeless state.
Having gone forth, he practiced all wholesome dharmas with courageous diligence;

because he applied himself so earnestly to the good, not long after his renunciation he attained the five supernormal powers, reaching the ultimate consummation and obtaining dharanis and uninterrupted, wondrous eloquence.

"After the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, by means of the power of the superknowledges and wisdom he had attained, he continued to turn the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata for ten intermediate kalpas."

For ten intermediate kalpas, the bhikṣu Candracchattra followed the turning of the wheel of Dharma and upheld the true Dharma with courageous diligence; he established hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings so that they attained non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he taught and transformed fourteen nayutas of beings so that their minds were well-tamed and compliant toward the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and through skillful means, he guided immeasurable sentient beings to be born in the heavens.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Was that Universal Monarch Ratnacchattra anyone else?
Do not give rise to doubt; do not view him as being another."
Why is this so? You should know that he is none other than the Tathāgata Ratnārcis.

The king’s thousand sons are the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa who will successively attain Buddhahood—the first to achieve Buddhahood shall be named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, and the last to achieve Buddhahood shall be named Ruci; four have already appeared in the world, while the remainder are yet to come.
At that time, was the prince Dharmapāla Candracchattra anyone else?
He was none other than myself.
O Lord of Devas, you should know this:
I declare that among all offerings made to the Buddhas, the offering of the Dharma is the most honored, the most excellent, the highest, the most sublime, and the unsurpassed.
"Therefore, O Śakra, Lord of Devas!
Those who wish to make offerings to the Buddha should do so through the offering of the Dharma;
do not use material wealth. Chapter 14: Entrustment At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

"I now entrust to you this Great Dharma that flows from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment accumulated by me over immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas."

Such a sutra as this—sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and protected by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power—you, too, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, shall sustain and uphold it through your own spiritual power during the evil age of the five turbidities, causing it to be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa so that it does not disappear or perish.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be sons of good family or daughters of good family, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others—who have already planted immeasurable and sublime roots of goodness, and who have developed a vast inclination and resolute conviction toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—if they do not hear such a sūtra as this, they will surely lose immeasurable benefits;
yet if they do hear such a sūtra as this, they will certainly believe and rejoice, giving rise to a sense of wonder and receiving it with joy upon their heads.

I now entrust those sons and daughters of good family to you; you should protect and keep them in mind so that they may be free from obstacles and hindrances as they hear, study, and practice this sutra, and so that this Dharma-gate thus taught may be widely proclaimed and spread.
“Maitreya, you should know that there are,
in brief, two kinds of seals of the characteristics of bodhisattvas. What are these two?
First, the seal of delighting in various ornate literary expressions; second, the seal of entering into the nature and characteristics of profound Dharma gates without fear.
If bodhisattvas revere, believe in, and delight in flowery and ornate rhetoric, it should be known that these are bodhisattvas who are beginners.

If bodhisattvas have no fear regarding this profound, untainted, unattached, inconceivable, and sovereignly miraculous dharma-gate of liberation—a subtle and wondrous sutra—and having heard it, they believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it until they have mastered it, extensively explain it to others, enter into it according to reality, and practice with diligence, thereby attaining supramundane, pure faith and delight, it should be known that these are bodhisattvas who are long-practiced.
“Maitreya, you should know that,
briefly stated, due to four conditions, a beginner bodhisattva brings about self-injury and is unable to attain profound dharma-patience.
What are these four?
First, upon first hearing a profound sutra never heard before, they become startled, terrified, and doubtful, failing to give rise to sympathetic joy;
second, having heard it, they slander and disparage it, saying:
"I have never heard this sutra before; from where has it come?"
"Third, seeing those sons of good family who uphold and expound this profound Dharma-gate, they do not delight in approaching, honoring, or prostrating before them;
fourth, at a later time, they treat them with contempt, malice, envy, insult, and slander."
Due to these four conditions, a beginner bodhisattva brings about self-injury and is unable to attain profound dharma-patience.
"Maitreya, you should know that briefly,

due to four conditions, a bodhisattva who resolves upon the profound gateway of the Dharma brings about self-injury and cannot quickly realize the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
What are these four?

First, to despise beginner bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the Mahāyāna and have not long practiced; second, to take no pleasure in receiving their guidance, instruction, and admonition; third, to lack deep respect for the profound and extensive training rules (*śikṣāpada*); and fourth, to prefer gathering sentient beings through worldly material gifts rather than through the supramundane gift of the pure Dharma.

"Due to these four conditions, a bodhisattva who seeks to understand this profound dharma-gate harms themselves and will not be able to swiftly realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having heard the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva Maitreya was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What the World-Honored One has spoken is most rare; what the Tathāgata has said is most subtle and wondrous."
I shall completely and utterly distance myself from all the faults of bodhisattvas as shown by the Buddha;

and I shall protect and uphold the Great Dharma that flows from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment accumulated by the Tathāgata over immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, ensuring it does not become obscured or extinguished.

If, in future ages, there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who seek to study the Mahāyāna and are true vessels for the Dharma, I shall cause them to obtain such profound sūtras as these in their own hands; I shall grant them the power of mindfulness so that they may receive, uphold, read, recite, master thoroughly, transcribe, honor, practice without error, and extensively explain this sūtra to others.
"Bhagavān!

If, in future ages, there should be those who hear this sutra, believe and understand it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, master it, practice it without error, and extensively explain it to others, you should know that all of these are sustained by my majestic spiritual power and protected by my empowerment."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent!
You have done very well indeed to rejoice in the Tathāgata’s skillful teaching and to embrace and uphold such true Dharma."
At that time, all the bodhisattvas present in the assembly—those from this world-system as well as those who had come from other directions—united their palms and spoke with one voice:
“World-Honored One!

We, too, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, shall each come from various other worlds in the ten directions to this place, to protect and uphold the Great Dharma flowing from the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment attained by the Tathāgata, so that it may not be obscured or extinguished, but widely proclaimed and disseminated.

If any son of good family or daughter of good family is able to hear, believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, recite, master thoroughly, practice without error, and extensively explain this sutra to others, I shall protect and sustain them, bestowing upon them the power of mindfulness so that they may be free from obstacles and difficulties.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings within this assembly also joined their palms and addressed the Buddha with one voice:
“World-Honored One!

Should there be villages, cities, towns, districts, or royal capitals—anywhere such a Dharma-gate circulates—we shall all go to those places together with our retinues and great powerful generals leading our military hosts, for the sake of hearing the Dharma. We shall protect and uphold such a spoken Dharma-gate, as well as those who can proclaim, receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-gate. Within a hundred *yojana* in the four directions, we shall ensure they are peaceful and secure, free from all obstacles and difficulties, and that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them shall find such an opening.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold this Dharma-gate, and extensively explain it to others so that it may be widely disseminated."
Ānanda said: "I have already received and upheld such a Dharma-gate,
World-Honored One!"
"What is the name of this Dharma-gate thus taught?
How should I uphold it?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This is called 'The Teaching on the Dharma-Gate of the Liberation of the Inconceivable Sovereign Supernatural Transformations of Vimalakīrti'; it should be upheld in this way.

When the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the venerable Ānanda, along with the other bodhisattvas, the great śrāvakas, and the assembly of devas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly delighted; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll Six.
